questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old male presents with progressive bulging of the right eye with a diminision of vision since 1 day. He has a history of URTI and on examination, it is seen that he also has nasal congestion with active discharge. The CT scan of the PNS is seen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sinusitis with subperiosteal abcess

In the given clinical scenario, a male patient with symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) exhibits opacity in the right ethmoidal sinus, as shown by the CT image, suggesting a probable diagnosis of sinusitis. CT scans show a typical lenticular rim-enhancing collection adjacent to the lamina papyracea with a fat plane between it and the displaced medial rectus muscle, suggesting a diagnosis of Sinusitis with subperiosteal abscess.

Orbital complications occur most commonly following ethmoid sinusitis as the ethmoid sinus is separated from the orbit by a thin papery bone known as lamina papyracea. Also, the venous supply of orbit and ethmoid sinuses is the same and additionally, these veins are valveless (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins). It can vary in degree and severity and is typically graded with the Chandler classification.

Chandler stages

Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Stage 5

Preseptal cellulitis

Postseptal cellulitis or orbital cellulitis without abscess

Subperiosteal abscess

Orbital abscess

Cavernous sinus thrombosis/abscess

Inflammation does not extend beyond the orbital septum (where the medial orbital periosteal reflection attaches to the medial eyelid at the tarsal plate).

Inflammation extends into the tissues of the orbit.

There is abscess formation deep to the periosteum of the orbital bones, typically at the lamina papyracea from ethmoid sinusitis.

There is abscess formation within the orbit which has breached the periosteum.

The inflammatory process has extended into the cavernous sinus which thromboses and may progress to abscess formation.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is advised as first-line imaging because of its superiority in demonstrating bony anatomy and pathology of the orbit and sinuses with its speed and ease of examination. MRI provides outstanding soft tissue detail without radiation exposure.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the major contributor to frailty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sarcopenia

Frailty is a geriatric syndrome characterized by reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors. Sarcopenia (age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength, and function) is the major biological contributor to frailty and is central to its pathogenesis.

Why is A correct?

• Sarcopenia leads to:

• Decreased muscle strength
• Reduced physical performance
• Increased risk of falls
• Functional dependence

• It is the primary contributor to the development and progression of frailty.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child is stung multiple times after disturbing a beehive and subsequently develops shock, respiratory distress, and circulatory collapse. Which mediator released during this reaction is mainly responsible for these life-threatening effects?
questions.explanation: The child is experiencing Anaphylaxis, a life-threatening, systemic Type I hypersensitivity reaction triggered by the bee venom antigens. Upon re-exposure, the venom binds to IgE antibodies on the surface of mast cells and basophils, leading to massive degranulation. The "primary mediator" responsible for the rapid onset of vascular collapse (hypotension) and respiratory distress (bronchoconstriction and laryngeal edema) is "Histamine". Histamine causes profound vasodilation and increased capillary permeability. Adrenaline (Option A) is the "treatment" of choice used to reverse these symptoms but is not the causative substance released by the body's immune cells during the reaction. Dopamine (Option C) and Substance P (Option D) are involved in various physiological signaling processes but are not the primary mediators of acute anaphylactic shock. Immediate administration of intramuscular epinephrine is mandatory to stabilize the patient's airway and blood pressure. Understanding these mediators is essential for both emergency management and the underlying principles of immunology and pathology

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with tingling in the lateral three fingers and loss of sensation at the base of the thumb on the dorsal hand. Which nerve is involved?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of tingling in the lateral digits and loss of sensation at the dorsal base of the thumb point to the superficial branch of the radial nerve. This nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsum of the hand, particularly the first web space and the dorsal aspect of the lateral three-and-a-half fingers, excluding the nail beds. The ulnar nerve (Option B) supplies the medial one-and-a-half digits and is not involved here. While the median nerve (Option C) supplies the lateral three-and-a-half digits, its distribution is primarily palmar and includes only the distal dorsal phalanges (fingertips); it does not supply the dorsal root of the thumb. The Anterior Interosseous Nerve (Option D) is a purely motor branch of the median nerve and has no cutaneous sensory distribution. Therefore, the specific loss of sensation on the dorsal aspect of the thumb base confirms radial nerve involvement

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The drug that binds to CD4 and has action on both CCR5 and CXCR4 in tropic HIV infections is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ibalizumab

The drug that binds to CD4 and has an action on both CCR5 and CXCR4 in tropic HIV infections is Ibalizumab.

Ibalizumab is an anti-CD4 monoclonal antibody approved for use in the treatment of multidrug-resistant HIV-1. It has action on both CCR5 and CXCR4 in tropic HIV infections and is administered intravenously.

It acts as an entry inhibitor. It blocks HIV-1 from infecting CD4+ T cells by binding to domain 2 of CD4 cells. It also interferes with post-attachment steps required for the entry of HIV-1 virus particles into host cells and thus prevents the viral transmission that occurs via cell-cell fusion.

Other options:

Option A: Maraviroc binds to the host cell CCR5 receptor to block the binding of viral gp120. It prevents the entry of the viral particles. It does not bind to CD4.

Option C: Elvitegravir is an integrase inhibitor that inhibits HIV 1 viral integrase enzyme and prevents proviral DNA integration into host cells.

Option D: Fosamprenavir is a protease inhibitor that blocks the viral protease enzyme necessary to produce mature virions upon budding from the host membrane.
questions.learning: Ibalizumab — The drug that binds to CD4 and has an action on both CCR5 and CXCR4 in tropic HIV infections is Ibalizumab. Ibalizumab is an anti-CD4 monoclonal antibody approved for use in the treatment of multidrug-resistant HIV-1.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following: Organism: 1. Helicobacter pylori 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis 3. Chlamydia trachomatis 4. Non-penicillinase-producing gonococci Drug: a. Amoxicillin b. Doxycycline c. Clarithromycin d. Streptomycin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1–c, 2–d, 3–b, 4–a

Knowledge of the drug of choice (DOC) for common bacterial pathogens is essential for selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy and is frequently tested in examinations.

Correct Match:

• 1. Helicobacter pylori → c. Clarithromycin
• 2. Mycobacterium tuberculosis → d. Streptomycin
• 3. Chlamydia trachomatis → b. Doxycycline
• 4. Non-penicillinase-producing gonococci → a. Amoxicillin (historically susceptible strains)

Why is A correct?

• H. pylori eradication regimens include clarithromycin (where macrolide resistance is low) along with a proton pump inhibitor and other antibiotics.
• Streptomycin is a first-line antitubercular drug (now mainly reserved for selected indications such as drug-resistant TB or when injectable agents are required).
• Doxycycline is the drug of choice for uncomplicated Chlamydia trachomatis infection.
• Non-penicillinase-producing Neisseria gonorrhoeae are susceptible to amoxicillin/penicillin; however, due to widespread resistance, ceftriaxone is now the recommended treatment in current practice.
questions.learning: 1–c, 2–d, 3–b, 4–a Knowledge of the drug of choice (DOC) for common bacterial pathogens is essential for selecting appropriate antimicrobial therapy and is frequently tested in examinations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with episodes of hematemesis following recent heavy alcohol consumption. He appears pale but is hemodynamically stable, with no ongoing bleeding at presentation. Liver function tests are within normal limits, and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is planned. Based on this clinical scenario, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, typically occurring after episodes of forceful retching or vomiting, often following heavy alcohol consumption. The patient’s stable vitals and normal liver function tests (LFTs) make esophageal varices (Option A) less likely, as varices are usually associated with portal hypertension and cirrhosis. Gastric ulcers (Option B) can cause hematemesis but are not specifically linked to acute alcohol-related retching cycles. While alcoholic gastritis (Option D) can cause erosive bleeding, it typically results in slower blood loss rather than acute hematemesis following vomiting episodes. The classic presentation of hematemesis following initially non-bloody emesis in an alcoholic patient is highly characteristic of a Mallory-Weiss tear. Diagnosis is confirmed by endoscopy, which usually reveals a linear tear near the Z-line. Most cases are self-limiting and managed conservatively with acid suppression, though endoscopic therapy may be needed for active bleeding or visible vessels
questions.learning: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction, typically occurring after episodes of forceful retching or vomiting, often following heavy alcohol consumption.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Peri-operative respiratory failure is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type III respiratory failure

Type III respiratory failure, also known as peri-operative respiratory failure, occurs due to reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis). It is commonly seen after major surgery, especially upper abdominal and thoracic procedures, because of anesthesia, pain, diaphragmatic dysfunction, and prolonged recumbency.

Why not the other options?

• A. Type I respiratory failure: Hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO₂ <60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO₂), seen in pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, and pulmonary embolism.
• B. Type II respiratory failure: Hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO₂ >50 mmHg), caused by alveolar hypoventilation (e.g., COPD, neuromuscular disorders, CNS depression).
• D. Type IV respiratory failure: Occurs in shock, where respiratory muscle hypoperfusion leads to ventilatory failure.
questions.learning: Type III respiratory failure Type III respiratory failure, also known as peri-operative respiratory failure, occurs due to reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) leading to alveolar collapse (atelectasis).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A municipality health officer reviews malaria data. State API = 0.7, but one district has API = 1.3. The SPR in that district suddenly doubled over 2 weeks. Which NVBDCP classification category applies to this state and what does the SPR specifically indicate?
options: Category 0 (Prevention of re-establishment); SPR = operational efficiency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Category 2 (Pre-elimination); SPR = outbreak indicator

NVBDCP state classification:

| Classification | State API | District API | Category

| -------------- | --------- | ------------ | --------

| Intensified Malaria Control | >1 | — | 3

| Pre-elimination | <1 | Few districts >1 | 2

| Elimination | <1 | <1 | 1

| Prevention of re-establishment | — | 0 | 0

State API = 0.7 (<1) BUT one district = 1.3 (>1) = Pre-elimination = Category 2.

Malaria indicators:

| Indicator | Formula | Measures

| --------- | ------- | --------

| API | Confirmed cases/Population × 1000 | Malaria prevalence

| ABER | Slides examined/Population × 100 | Fever prevalence (operational efficiency)

| SPR | Slides +ve/Slides examined × 100 | Outbreak indicator

Sudden doubling of SPR = outbreak signal, not prevalence trend.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient has undergone a gastrectomy (partial or total removal of the stomach) and is being monitored for postoperative complications and nutritional changes. Which condition is most likely to develop as a direct result of this surgery?
questions.explanation: A direct and major consequence of total or subtotal gastrectomy is the development of Vitamin B12 deficiency . The stomach’s parietal cells secrete Intrinsic Factor (IF), which is essential for the absorption of Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum. Once the stomach or its secreting mucosa is removed, the patient can no longer absorb dietary B12, eventually leading to megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord if not supplemented. Folic acid (Option A) is absorbed primarily in the small intestine and is less specifically affected by the loss of the stomach. Gastric ulcers (Option C) are what the surgery often treats, and constipation (Option D) is not a specific metabolic consequence of gastrectomy compared to the profound risk of B12 malabsorption. Therefore, lifelong intramuscular Vitamin B12 injections are a mandatory component of postoperative care for gastrectomy patients. Recognition of this risk allows for the prevention of irreversible neurological damage
questions.learning: A direct and major consequence of total or subtotal gastrectomy is the development of Vitamin B12 deficiency . The stomach’s parietal cells secrete Intrinsic Factor (IF), which is essential for the absorption of Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which method is used to separate Bajra grains from black seeds when they are mixed together?
questions.explanation: The separation of bajra (pearl millet) grains from black seeds is based on the principle of difference in density (specific gravity). When the mixture is placed in a 10% salt solution, the density of the liquid increases compared to plain water. In this medium: 1. 1. Heavier bajra grains have a higher density than the salt solution → they sink 2. 2. Lighter black seeds (impurities/weed seeds) have a lower density → they float This allows easy separation by decantation or skimming off the floating particles. A 10% salt solution is optimal because it provides the right density difference for effective separation. If the solution is too dilute (like water or normal saline), both may sink. If too concentrated, even desired grains might float, reducing efficiency. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 20% salt water: Too concentrated → may float both components (B) Normal saline (~0.9%): Too dilute → ineffective separation (D) Water: No sufficient density difference
questions.learning: The separation of bajra (pearl millet) grains from black seeds is based on the principle of difference in density (specific gravity). When the mixture is placed in a 10% salt solution, the density of the liquid increases compared to plain water.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the WHO classification of astrocytoma, which specific grade is glioblastoma categorized as?
questions.explanation: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of tumors of the central nervous system, astrocytomas are graded from I to IV based on their degree of malignancy and histological features. Glioblastoma (previously known as glioblastoma multiforme) is the most aggressive and lethal form, and it is definitively categorized as Grade IV. Grade I refers to benign, localized tumors like pilocytic astrocytoma. Grade II (Option B) are low-grade diffuse astrocytomas. Grade III (Option C) are anaplastic astrocytomas, which are malignant but less aggressive than glioblastoma. Grade IV tumors like glioblastoma are characterized by high mitotic activity, nuclear atypia, and pathognomonic features such as microvascular proliferation and/or necrosis. These tumors are highly invasive and have a very poor prognosis despite aggressive therapy. Therefore, Grade IV is the standard classification for glioblastoma in both academic and clinical settings
questions.learning: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of tumors of the central nervous system, astrocytomas are graded from I to IV based on their degree of malignancy and histological features.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the fistula labeled below:
questions.explanation: The provided anatomical diagram illustrates an abnormal communication (fistula) between the posterior wall of the urinary bladder and the anterior wall of the vagina. This specific connection defines a Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF). VVF is a common obstetric injury in developing nations, typically resulting from prolonged obstructed labor, or it can occur as an iatrogenic complication of gynecological surgery. A Vesicocervical fistula (Option A) would connect the bladder to the cervix. A Urethrovaginal fistula (Option B) connects the urethra to the vagina, located much lower than the bladder neck. A Ureterovaginal fistula (Option C) involves the ureter. Because the diagram clearly marks the "Bladder" as one end and the "Vagina" as the other, the diagnosis is definitively VVF. Patients typically present with continuous, involuntary leakage of urine into the vagina
questions.learning: The provided anatomical diagram illustrates an abnormal communication (fistula) between the posterior wall of the urinary bladder and the anterior wall of the vagina.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following statements are true regarding Wilm's tumour except?
options: It presents most commonly as abdominal mass
Most common age of presentation is within 5 years
95% of patients live long term with radiotherapy and chemotherapy
Metastasis to lungs is rare and occurs late
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 95% of patients live long term with radiotherapy and chemotherapy

Option C is not true regarding Wilms tumour. The standard treatment of Wilm's tumour involves a combination of chemotherapy and surgery.

Wilms tumor is the most common primary malignant renal tumor in children, typically affecting children less than 5 years ( OptionB). After neuroblastoma, it is the second most common malignant abdominal tumor in childhood. It most commonly presents as an asymptomatic abdominal mass. (Option A) Other findings include hypertension, abdominal pain, gross painless hematuria, and constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss.

CECT abdomen is used to identify the extent of the tumor, integrity of the other kidney, and metastasis. Wilms tumor is metabolically active and can concentrate fluorodeoxyglucose therefore PET/CT is also helpful to identify regional spread and metastatic lesions. A biopsy is discouraged as it may lead to disease upstaging.

Treatment: Surgery and chemotherapy, with or without radiotherapy, are the mainstays of treatment.

• Radical nephrectomy is the standard surgical procedure done. Routine sampling of the para-aortic, hilar, and paracaval lymph nodes should be done.
• Nephron-sparing nephrectomy is done for children with bilateral disease or with a solitary kidney. Preoperative chemotherapy can be used in these cases to induce tumor shrinkage.
• The classical chemotherapy includes vincristine and dactinomycin with the addition of Adriamycin(Doxorubicin).

Despite certain adverse risk factors such as metastases, unfavorable histology and recurrent disease, the prognosis for most children with Wilms' tumor remains very positive. The overall survival rate for children with Wilms' tumor is over 90%.

The tumour can extend into the renal vein and vena cava and metastasises to lymph nodes and lung. But metastasis to lungs occur late in the disease. (Option D)
questions.learning: 95% of patients live long term with radiotherapy and chemotherapy Option C is not true regarding Wilms tumour. The standard treatment of Wilm's tumour involves a combination of chemotherapy and surgery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother brings her child to the pediatric outpatient department complaining of recurrent infections. On examination, her child has a length-for-age less than–2 standard deviations below the median. There is a history of improper feeding in the past. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stunting

A length-for-age less than –2 standard deviations (SD) below the median is called stunting according to WHO.

Classification of nutritional status depending on the anthropometry (height/length for age):

Classification
Criteria

Moderate stunting (or) moderate chronic malnutrition
Height/length-for-age < –2 SD and > –3 SD

Severe stunting (or) severe chronic malnutrition
Height/length-for-age < –3 SD

The nutritional status of a child is assessed in terms of anthropometry:

The World Health Organization (WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. It is also mentioned as wasting.

* High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

* Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight-for-age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Other options:

Option A: To diagnose a child as underweight, weight for age charts are used. If the weight for the age of a child is less than -2 SD, then the child is said to be moderately underweight. If it is less than -3SD, it is called severe underweight.

Option B: A diagnosis of wasting can be made with mid-upper arm circumference measurements and weight for height. A weight for height below -2 SD is called moderate wasting. A mid-upper arm circumference of less than 115mm or weight for height below -3SD is called severe wasting.

Option C: Malnutrition refers to any deficiencies in the dietary intake of a person. Although it means both undernutrition and overnutrition, in practice it is used interchangeably with undernutrition.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 50-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is started on lifestyle modification. After a few weeks, his insulin sensitivity improves, leading to increased glucose uptake in peripheral tissues. Which of the following transporters is primarily responsible for this insulin-mediated glucose uptake?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GLUT4 in skeletal muscle

Insulin-mediated glucose uptake in peripheral tissues is primarily via GLUT4.

• GLUT4:

• Found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue
• Insulin-dependent transporter
• Insulin → translocation of GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to cell membrane → ↑ glucose uptake

• Other GLUTs (important contrasts):

• GLUT1 → RBCs, basal uptake (insulin-independent)
• GLUT2 → liver, pancreas (high Km, bidirectional)
• GLUT3 → neurons (high affinity, insulin-independent)

• Clinical relevance:

• In type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance → ↓ GLUT4 translocation
• Exercise and lifestyle changes improve GLUT4 activity → ↑ insulin sensitivity
questions.learning: GLUT4 in skeletal muscle Insulin-mediated glucose uptake in peripheral tissues is primarily via GLUT4. • GLUT4: • Found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue • Insulin-dependent transporter • Insulin → translocation of GLUT4 from intracellular vesicles to…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: During fasting, through which metabolic pathway does glucagon stimulate the production of glucose?
questions.explanation: During a fasting state, blood glucose levels drop, triggering the secretion of glucagon from the pancreatic alpha cells. Glucagon acts primarily on the liver to elevate blood glucose through two key metabolic pathways. First, it stimulates glycogenolysis, which is the breakdown of stored glycogen into glucose. Second, it promotes gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors like amino acids and glycerol. Glycolysis (Option A) is the breakdown of glucose to produce energy and is inhibited by glucagon to conserve glucose. Glycogenesis (Option C) is the synthesis of glycogen for storage, which occurs in the fed state under the influence of insulin. While gluconeogenesis (Option D) is a major contributor, it does not work alone; both pathways are essential for glucose homeostasis during fasting. Therefore, the combination of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis is the correct physiological response to glucagon
questions.learning: During a fasting state, blood glucose levels drop, triggering the secretion of glucagon from the pancreatic alpha cells. Glucagon acts primarily on the liver to elevate blood glucose through two key metabolic pathways.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most appropriate first-line medication for a 9-year-old girl who experiences frequent, brief staring spells, occasional chewing movements, and daydreaming, leading to declining academic performance, with no loss of posture or generalized convulsions, and corresponding EEG findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of brief staring spells, subtle automatisms (chewing), and declining school performance in a child is pathognomonic for Absence Seizures. The provided EEG confirms this, showing the classic 3 Hz spike-and-wave pattern. Sodium valproate (Option C) and Ethosuximide are the first-line initial medications for this condition. While Ethosuximide is often preferred for pure absence seizures, Valproate is highly effective and frequently the answer in general clinical exams. Carbamazepine (Option A) and Phenytoin (Option B) are strictly contraindicated for absence seizures as they can paradoxically worsen the frequency of attacks. Clonazepam (Option D) is a benzodiazepine that can be used as an adjunct but is not the primary long-term therapy. Therefore, because Valproate effectively suppresses the 3 Hz cortical discharges, it is the definitive initial choice. Correct management is essential to restore the child's academic function and prevent daily staring episodes
questions.learning: The clinical description of brief staring spells, subtle automatisms (chewing), and declining school performance in a child is pathognomonic for Absence Seizures.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient was brought by the police in an unconscious state to the casualty with a history of unknown poisoning. On examination, the patient had needle track marks over the upper limbs. He also had increased blood pressure, increased heart rate and hyperthermia. Which poisoning should be suspected here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cocaine

The history of poisoning with hypertension, tachycardia and hyperthermia is suggestive of cocaine poisoning.

Track marks are visible signs on the skin, typically scars or puncture wounds, resulting from repeated intravenous drug injections, commonly associated with substance abuse.

Cocaine is an alkaloid deliriant extracted from Erythroxylum coca.

Acute intoxication with cocaine leads to symptoms spanning 2 stages-

* Stage of excitement/euphoria - associated with hypervigilance, anxiety, hyperactivity along with hyper-adrenergic signs of mydriasis, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, hyperthermia, and cardiac arrhythmias.

* Stage of depression - associated with loss of reflexes, muscle paralysis, circulatory and respiratory failure, and coma.

Toxic delirium and tactile hallucinations—also referred to as "cocaine bugs" or formication—are hallmarks of chronic intoxication. The sensation of insects creeping under the skin is known as formication.

Common complications include cerebrovascular accidents and myocardial ischemia.

Treatment includes intravenous diazepam for controlling seizures. For ventricular arrhythmias, propranolol may be given intravenously. If the patient has psychosis, haloperidol may be given. Treatment of chronic cocaine abuse requires psychiatric support.

Following an abrupt cessation of long-term cocaine use, cocaine withdrawal occurs. The phases are as follows -

* Crash phase (9 hours - 96 hours): Anorexia, depression, excessive craving, hypersomnia, fatigue.

* Normal mood, anxiety, and anhedonia (4 - 7 days)

* Extinction phase (7 - 10 days): Absence of withdrawal symptoms but increased susceptibility to relapse.

Treatment for withdrawal includes bromocriptine and amantadine. They are useful in reducing cocaine craving.

Chronic: Runs & crashes, choreiform movements, tooth decay. Can resemble schizophrenia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 75-year-old female presented with urinary incontinence. She also has cognition decline and dementia. Which of the following drugs is useful for treating urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tolterodine

For managing urinary incontinence in a 75-year-old female with cognitive decline and dementia, tolterodine is useful.

Tolterodine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist specifically effective for treating urinary incontinence. It exhibits selectivity for the urinary bladder, which helps to minimize side effects compared to other antimuscarinic agents. This selectivity is beneficial for patients with cognitive decline or dementia, as it reduces the risk of adverse effects. Tolterodine is metabolized by CYP2D6, so its dosage may need adjustment based on individual CYP2D6 activity, making it a suitable option for managing urinary incontinence while minimizing potential side effects.

Other muscarinic antagonists for urinary incontinence include oxybutynin, trospium chloride, darifenacin, solifenacin, and fesoterodine. Oxybutynin, though effective, often causes antimuscarinic side effects such as xerostomia. Trospium chloride, being a quaternary amine, is better tolerated and excreted primarily via the kidneys, requiring dosage adjustments in renal impairment. Darifenacin and solifenacin have selectivity for M3 receptors, which helps balance efficacy and side effects, while fesoterodine, a prodrug, provides a stable pharmacokinetic profile due to its conversion to tolterodine’s active metabolite.

Other Options:

Option A: Tiotropium and Option C: Ipratropium are muscarinic antagonists used primarily for respiratory conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and asthma, rather than urinary incontinence. Tiotropium is a long-acting agent with selectivity for M1 and M3 receptors, while Ipratropium is used more frequently for its short-acting effects.

Option D: Telenzepine, an analogue of Pirenzepine, displays higher potency and selectivity for M1 receptors compared to pirenzepine and is used in treating acid-peptic disease, not urinary incontinence.
questions.learning: Tolterodine For managing urinary incontinence in a 75-year-old female with cognitive decline and dementia, tolterodine is useful. Tolterodine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist specifically effective for treating urinary incontinence.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A child is starting to walk and gain upright posture. Which of the following spinal curvatures develops secondarily due to the development of this function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lumbar

Lumbar curvature develops secondarily when the child starts walking and gaining upright posture.

During embryonic life, the body appears flexed and has 2 primary spinal curvatures.These are the thoracic and the pelvic curves, which are convex dorsally.

After birth, functional muscle development leads to the early appearance of secondary spinal curvatures. These are the cervical and the lumbar curves, both of which are convex forwards (lordosis).

* The secondary cervical curvature occurs with the development of function in the muscles responsible for the head extension.

* The secondary lumbar curvature occurs with the development of function in the muscles responsible for sitting upright and walking.

Normal adult curvatures of the vertebral column are as follows:

* The cervical curve is lordosis (convex forwards)

* The thoracic curve is kyphosis (convex dorsally)

* The lumbar curve is lordosis (convex forwards)

* The pelvic curve is concave anteroinferiorly
questions.learning: Lumbar Lumbar curvature develops secondarily when the child starts walking and gaining upright posture. During embryonic life, the body appears flexed and has 2 primary spinal curvatures.These are the thoracic and the pelvic curves, which are convex dorsally.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man is brought to the emergency department after falling from a height with his hand outstretched. X-ray shows a clavicular fracture. Which part of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd

The junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd (middle third) of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured.

The middle third of the clavicle is the narrowest and has the least amount of surrounding soft tissue structures. Therefore, most fractures (~80%) are seen in the middle third.

Fall on the shoulder (direct impact) and fall on the outstretched hand are the most common causes of clavicle fracture.

The patient will be presented with the flexed elbow as the arm will be held to the chest to prevent movement. It is divided into three based on the location of the fractures:

* Group I – middle-third fractures

* Group II – lateral-third fractures

* Group III – medial-third fractures
questions.learning: Junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd — The junction of medial 2/3rd and lateral 1/3rd (middle third) of the clavicle is most likely to be fractured.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following carcinomas is least likely to be seen in a patient on oral contraceptives?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial cancer

Oral contraceptive pills (OCP) protect against endometrial carcinomas. This effect is thought to be due to the opposition of estrogen induces proliferation by progestins in OCP. They also decrease the incidence of ovarian and colorectal cancers.

Other benefits of oral contraceptive pills:

* Regularisation of menstrual cycles results in relief of dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia

* Reduced incidence of fibrocystic breast disease and ovarian cysts

* Endometriosis and pelvic inflammatory disease are improved

On the other hand, OCP increase the incidence of hepatic adenomas , HCC and breast cancers.
questions.learning: Endometrial cancer Oral contraceptive pills (OCP) protect against endometrial carcinomas. This effect is thought to be due to the opposition of estrogen induces proliferation by progestins in OCP.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The single most important treatment and prognostic factor in alcohol-related liver disease is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cessation of alcohol consumption

Complete abstinence from alcohol is the single most important treatment and the strongest predictor of long-term survival in patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD), irrespective of the stage of liver disease. Abstinence halts ongoing hepatocyte injury, improves liver function, reduces portal hypertension, and decreases the risk of progression to cirrhosis, hepatic decompensation, and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Why not the other options?

• A. N-acetylcysteine (NAC): Primarily used for acetaminophen toxicity; may be used as an adjunct in severe alcoholic hepatitis with corticosteroids but is not the cornerstone of treatment.
• C. Liver transplantation: Reserved for end-stage liver disease or selected patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis who fail medical therapy; it is not the first-line treatment.
• D. High-dose vitamin E: Has a role in selected patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), not alcohol-related liver disease.
questions.learning: Cessation of alcohol consumption Complete abstinence from alcohol is the single most important treatment and the strongest predictor of long-term survival in patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALD), irrespective of the stage of liver disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A female from Himachal Pradesh presented with H/O thorn prick, a year back has a verrucous lesion in the skin with the following microscopic findings. Identify the agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

The given clinical history and histopathological image are suggestive of Chromoblastomycosis

Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation.

Over months to years, the primary lesion becomes verrucous and wart-like with extension along the draining lymphatics.

Histologically, the lesions are granulomatous and the dark sclerotic bodies may be seen within leukocytes or giant cells (medlar/copper penny bodies)

The following are the various dematiaceous species of fungi

• Phialophora verrucosa
• Fonsecaea pedrosoi
• Fonsecaea compacta
• Rhinocladiella aquaspersa
• Cladophialophora carrionii

Treatment: Surgical excision with wide margins is the treatment of choice for small lesions. Chemotherapy with flucytosine or itraconazole may be efficacious for larger lesions. The application of local heat is also beneficial.
questions.learning: Chromoblastomycosis — The given clinical history and histopathological image are suggestive of Chromoblastomycosis Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a subcutaneous mycotic infection that is usually caused by traumatic inoculation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with symptoms of eye strain. An image demonstrates that light rays are focused at different points along different meridians of the eye. Which refractive error best explains this finding?
questions.explanation: The provided image illustrates Sturm's conoid, a diagnostic optical phenomenon characteristic of astigmatism. In astigmatism, parallel light rays do not converge at a single focal point due to unequal refractive power in different meridians of the cornea or lens. Instead, they form two distinct focal lines at different planes. The area between these lines is the Sturm's conoid, and the point of relatively clear vision is the "circle of least confusion". This error leads to blurred vision and eye strain (asthenopia). Amblyopia (Option A) is a developmental reduction in vision unrelated to acute focusing errors. Hypermetropia (Option B) involves light focusing at a single point behind the retina. Presbyopia (Option D) is an age-related loss of accommodation affecting near vision but does not create multiple focal lines. Thus, the presence of two focal planes confirms astigmatism
questions.learning: The provided image illustrates Sturm's conoid, a diagnostic optical phenomenon characteristic of astigmatism. In astigmatism, parallel light rays do not converge at a single focal point due to unequal refractive power in different meridians of the cornea…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is used to clean up blood spills in the operation theater?
questions.explanation: Effective decontamination of blood spills in high-risk areas like operation theaters is critical for preventing the transmission of bloodborne pathogens such as HIV and Hepatitis. Sodium hypochlorite, a chlorine compound, is the globally recommended disinfectant for this purpose. For large spills, a 1% (10,000 ppm) concentration is typically used to ensure complete inactivation of infectious agents. Phenolic compounds (Option B) are less effective against some viruses and are generally used for surface disinfection of walls or floors. Quaternary ammonium compounds (Option C) are low-level disinfectants and are not suitable for blood spills. Alcoholic compounds (Option D), while useful for skin antisepsis, evaporate too quickly to provide the necessary contact time for organic matter like blood. Therefore, due to its potent virucidal properties and ability to neutralize organic biohazards, a chlorine-based compound is the gold standard for managing blood spills in clinical settings
questions.learning: Effective decontamination of blood spills in high-risk areas like operation theaters is critical for preventing the transmission of bloodborne pathogens such as HIV and Hepatitis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Basophils are activated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IL-5

Basophils are activated by IL-5 and IL-3.

Note: IL-5 primarily activates eosinophils.
questions.learning: IL-5 Basophils are activated by IL-5 and IL-3. Note: IL-5 primarily activates eosinophils.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child is diagnosed with amblyopia affecting the right eye. To promote visual development in the weaker eye, which management option is most appropriate to recommend?
options: Spectacles or refraction with a near addition
questions.explanation: Amblyopia, often called "lazy eye," is a developmental disorder where the brain fails to process inputs from one eye, favoring the other. At age three, the visual system is still plastic, making early intervention critical. Occlusion therapy, which involves patching the stronger "good" eye for several hours a day, is the gold-standard treatment. By forcing the brain to use the weaker, amblyopic eye, it stimulates the development of the corresponding visual cortex. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate as amblyopia does not resolve spontaneously and can lead to permanent vision loss. While refractive correction (Option B) is often the first step if an error exists, it is frequently insufficient on its own and must be followed by patching. Radial keratotomy (Option D) is an obsolete refractive surgery for myopia and is never used in pediatric amblyopia management. Therefore, occlusion therapy remains the most effective and widely used method to restore balanced vision in young children before the critical period of visual development ends around age seven to nine
questions.learning: Amblyopia, often called "lazy eye," is a developmental disorder where the brain fails to process inputs from one eye, favoring the other. At age three, the visual system is still plastic, making early intervention critical.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with the eyeball positioned down and out. Which cranial nerve palsy is most likely present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Third nerve palsy

Third nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy results in a characteristic “down and out” eye position due to unopposed action of:

• Lateral rectus (CN VI) → abducts eye
• Superior oblique (CN IV) → depresses and intorts

Key features:

• Eye deviated down and out
• Ptosis (levator palpebrae paralysis)
• Dilated pupil (parasympathetic involvement)
• Loss of adduction, elevation, and depression

Why not others:

• Sixth nerve → only abduction defect
• Fourth nerve → vertical diplopia, head tilt
• Seventh nerve → facial muscle involvement
questions.learning: Third nerve palsy Third nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy results in a characteristic “down and out” eye position due to unopposed action of: • Lateral rectus (CN VI) → abducts eye • Superior oblique (CN IV) → depresses and intorts Key features: • Eye…

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden irresistible urges to do things that come to his mind. Which of the following best describes this symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Impulse

The sudden irresistible urge to do things is called impulse.

They arise from intrusive thoughts the person has. These uncontrollable impulses seem rewarding to the subject. The person aims for immediate gratification and relief by just performing the act than from the after-effects. If the impulsive action has consequences in the long term, they tend to neglect these consequences. Often after acting on the impulse, the subject feels remorse and guilt. This in turn can lead to marked distress in the personal, family, social, and educational spheres.

Repeated failure to resist an impulse is the characteristic feature of impulse control disorder. They include

* Pyromania

* Kleptomania

* Compulsive sexual behavior disorder

* Intermittent explosive disorder

Option a: hallucination refers to a disorder of perception where there is perception without any stimuli.

Option b: illusion is another disorder of perception where a stimulus is perceived as something different,

Option c: delusion refers to false unshakable believes that arent in line with the socioeconomic background of the subject.
questions.learning: Impulse — The sudden irresistible urge to do things is called impulse. They arise from intrusive thoughts the person has.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which investigation is considered the most appropriate for diagnosing distal bowel tumors?
questions.explanation: Enteroclysis is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosing distal small bowel tumors because it provides excellent distension and detailed visualization of the small intestine mucosa. In this technique, contrast material is directly infused into the small bowel through a nasojejunal tube, allowing precise detection of subtle lesions, strictures, and tumors, especially in distal segments like the ileum. Its high sensitivity makes it superior to routine contrast studies. Other options are less suitable: (B) Barium meal primarily evaluates the esophagus, stomach, and proximal duodenum, so it cannot adequately visualize distal small bowel tumors. (C) Barium meal follow-through does examine the small intestine, but it is less sensitive and less detailed because contrast passes naturally, leading to poor distension and missed lesions. (D) Barium enema is used to study the large intestine (colon and rectum) and has no role in assessing small bowel tumors. Thus, due to its superior imaging quality and diagnostic accuracy for distal small bowel lesions, enteroclysis is the best choice
questions.learning: Enteroclysis is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosing distal small bowel tumors because it provides excellent distension and detailed visualization of the small intestine mucosa.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man’s chest X-ray shows bilateral blunting of the costophrenic angles along with a meniscus sign on the lateral view. Which condition is most consistent with these radiographic findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical hallmarks of a Pleural Effusion on a chest radiograph are the blunting of the costophrenic angle (where the lung meets the diaphragm) and the meniscus sign. The meniscus sign is a concave upper border of the fluid, created by the fluid climbing higher at the periphery due to capillary action and negative intrathoracic pressure. Emphysema (Option A) would show hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms. Tension pneumothorax (Option B) would show a dark, air-filled pleural space without lung markings and a shifted mediastinum. Bronchiectasis (Option D) typically shows "tram-track" opacities or cystic changes, not localized fluid collection in the base. Therefore, the specific combination of angle blunting and a radiographic meniscus is definitive for fluid in the pleural cavity. Bilateral involvement in a 65-year-old often suggests a systemic cause like congestive heart failure
questions.learning: The clinical hallmarks of a Pleural Effusion on a chest radiograph are the blunting of the costophrenic angle (where the lung meets the diaphragm) and the meniscus sign.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What stage of embryonic development is shown in the following image?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates a blastocyst, which typically forms around Day 5 of embryonic development. It is identifiable by its unique structure: an outer layer of cells called the trophoblast (which forms the placenta), a cluster of cells inside called the inner cell mass (which becomes the embryo), and a central fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel. A morula (Option A) is an earlier stage (Day 4) consisting of a solid ball of 16–32 cells without a cavity. An ovum (Option B) is the single-cell unfertilized egg. A gastrula (Option D) is a later stage (Day 14+) where the embryo differentiates into three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Implantation into the endometrial wall begins as the blastocyst stage is reached. Understanding these distinct morphological stages is fundamental for studying embryogenesis
questions.learning: The image illustrates a blastocyst, which typically forms around Day 5 of embryonic development. It is identifiable by its unique structure: an outer layer of cells called the trophoblast (which forms the placenta), a cluster of cells inside called the…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the given diagram of LV pressure-volume loop, point C represents
questions.explanation: In a left ventricular (LV) pressure–volume loop, point C represents the moment when the aortic valve opens. This occurs at the end of isovolumetric contraction, when the pressure inside the left ventricle rises high enough to exceed the pressure in the aorta. As a result, the aortic valve opens and the ejection phase begins, allowing blood to flow into the aorta. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Mitral valve closes : This event occurs at the beginning of isovolumetric contraction (point B), when ventricular pressure just exceeds left atrial pressure—not at point C. (C) Aortic valve closes : This happens at the end of ventricular ejection (point D), when ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, marking the start of isovolumetric relaxation. (D) Mitral valve opens : This occurs after isovolumetric relaxation (point A), when ventricular pressure drops below left atrial pressure, allowing ventricular filling. Thus, point C corresponds to aortic valve opening, making (B) the correct answer
questions.learning: In a left ventricular (LV) pressure–volume loop, point C represents the moment when the aortic valve opens. This occurs at the end of isovolumetric contraction, when the pressure inside the left ventricle rises high enough to exceed the pressure in the aorta.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is wrongly labelled here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C-Subscapular artery

The option marked C is wrongly labelled as it is the brachial artery and not subscapular artery.

The axillary artery is divided into 3 parts by the pectoralis minor muscle.

The axillary artery is the continuation of the subclavian artery. It extends from the outer border of 1st rib to the lower border of Teres Major.

Pectoralis Minor divides the artery into 3 parts (proximal to, posterior to and lateral to the muscle) and it continues as the brachial artery in the arm.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with a breast lump that was surgically excised, and the histopathological examination findings are provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The microscopic examination reveals clusters of malignant cells "floating" within abundant pools of extracellular mucin, which is the hallmark of mucinous (colloid) carcinoma of the breast. This rare subtype of invasive ductal carcinoma typically affects postmenopausal women and generally carries a more favorable prognosis. Lobular carcinoma (Option A) characteristically shows a "single-file" infiltration pattern due to the loss of E-cadherin. Medullary carcinoma (Option B) presents with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and a syncytial growth pattern but lacks mucin pools. Phyllodes tumor (Option D) is a fibroepithelial lesion characterized by leaf-like stromal projections and hypercellularity rather than extracellular mucin. Therefore, the distinct appearance of mucin-filled spaces confirms the diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma
questions.learning: The microscopic examination reveals clusters of malignant cells "floating" within abundant pools of extracellular mucin, which is the hallmark of mucinous (colloid) carcinoma of the breast.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The instrument shown in the image is used to insufflate the abdomen for laparoscopic surgery. What is its name?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Veress needle

The instrument shown in the image is the Veress needle which is used to insufflate the abdomen for laparoscopic surgery.

The image below shows the Veress needle:

There are two methods for establishing abdominal access during laparoscopic surgeries:

• Direct puncture using a Veress needle
• Direct peritoneal access (Hasson's technique)

Direct puncture laparoscopy:

In this procedure, first, the abdominal wall is grasped with towel clips or fingers to elevate it away from the underlying structures. Then, a small incision is made in the umbilicus, and insufflation is performed using a Veress needle. When introducing the Veress needle, two distinct pops can be felt as the needle pierces the abdominal wall fascia first and then the peritoneum. The umbilicus is the preferred location for introducing a Veress needle because the abdominal wall is thinner at this site.

Laparoscopic surgeries can be performed under general anesthesia or local anesthesia; although, general anesthesia is preferred. Carbon dioxide gas is usually used for insufflation, and the maximum pressure is typically in the range of 14-15 mm Hg. However, if the procedure is done under local anesthesia, nitrous oxide is used. Insufflation with nitrous oxide is stopped at a pressure of 10 mmHg or when 2L of gas has been insufflated.

Direct peritoneal access technique (Hasson technique): The surgeon makes a small umbilical incision and gains access to the peritoneal cavity under direct vision by dissecting through the abdominal fascia and peritoneum. It is preferred in patients who have undergone previous abdominal operations where the small bowel may be adherent to the undersurface of the abdominal wound.
questions.learning: Veress needle — The instrument shown in the image is the Veress needle which is used to insufflate the abdomen for laparoscopic surgery. The image below shows the Veress needle: There are two methods for establishing abdominal access during laparoscopic…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient is diagnosed with gouty arthritis. What biochemical changes will be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urate and lactate levels

This patient with chronic alcoholism and gouty arthritis will most likely have elevated levels of lactate and urate.

The oxidation of ethanol to acetate by alcohol dehydrogenase is accompanied by the reduction of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to NADH. This results in a high concentration of NADH, leading to an increased NADH/NAD+ ratio (Option A).

Due to this, the following metabolic reactions that require NAD+ are inhibited:

1. Glycolysis
2. Citric acid cycle (ketogenesis favored)
3. Pyruvate dehydrogenase
4. Fatty acid oxidation

Decreased fatty acid oxidation leads to increased esterification and production of triacylglycerol, which causes fatty liver.

Also, there is an increase in two reactions:

• Pyruvate to lactate
• Oxaloacetate to malate

Increased lactate leads to hyper-lactic-acidemia, which leads to increased renal reabsorption of urate and decreased excretion of uric acid. This results in aggravation of gout. Alcoholics are deficient in thiamine which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and leads to lactic acidosis.

A decrease in pyruvate and oxaloacetate levels, which are substrates for gluconeogenesis, leads to a decrease in blood glucose levels, causing symptoms of agitation, impaired judgment, and combativeness.

Other options:

Increased urea and urate levels are not specifically associated with alcoholism and gouty arthritis. While urate levels may be increased due to gout, urea levels are not directly related to the condition (Option B).

Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase can be seen in alcohol-induced hepatitis due to intrahepatic cholestasis but is not directly related to gouty arthritis in a chronic alcoholic patient. Therefore, this option is less relevant compared to increased urate and lactate levels (Option D).
questions.learning: Increased urate and lactate levels — This patient with chronic alcoholism and gouty arthritis will most likely have elevated levels of lactate and urate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a rural farming community, residents have developed allergic respiratory issues and contact dermatitis after exposure to a particular plant, and both humans and cattle show signs of mutagenicity upon contact. Which plant species, considered a noxious weed across America, Asia, Africa, and Australia, fits this description?
questions.explanation: The description provided identifies the highly invasive weed Parthenium hysterophorus (commonly known as "Congress grass" or "Carrot grass"). This plant is an aggressive noxious weed that has spread globally across America, Asia, Africa, and Australia. It contains potent allergens, such as parthenin, which cause severe contact dermatitis and allergic respiratory issues (asthma, hay fever) in humans. Additionally, it is toxic to livestock and has documented mutagenic and carcinogenic properties . Datura (Option B), Digitalis (Option C), and Calotropis (Option D) are well-known medicinal and poisonous plants, but they are not categorized as the specific "noxious invasive weed" responsible for widespread agricultural loss and systemic ecological dominance described in the scenario. Therefore, because of its unique status as a global environmental and public health hazard, Parthenium is the correct plant species
questions.learning: The description provided identifies the highly invasive weed Parthenium hysterophorus (commonly known as "Congress grass" or "Carrot grass"). This plant is an aggressive noxious weed that has spread globally across America, Asia, Africa, and Australia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the most common drawback of the given device?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Drug deposition in the oropharynx

The given image shows a metered-dose inhaler (MDI). The most common side effect of this device is drug deposition in the oropharynx.

Most material inhaled using this device will be swallowed and absorbed, entering systemic circulation after undergoing the first-pass effect in the liver. Some drug will also be absorbed into the systemic circulation from the lungs.

The use of a large-volume spacer will reduce the amount of drug deposited in the oropharynx, thereby reducing the amount swallowed and absorbed from the GI tract, thus limiting the systemic effects of the drug.

The given image shows the use of spacer with MDI:

Spacers reduce the velocity and size of particles entering the upper airways. This reduces the amount of drug that impinges on the oropharynx and increases the proportion of the drug inhaled into the lower airways.

Spacer devices are useful in delivering inhaled drugs to small children, as young as 3 years of age, who are not able to use a pMDI (pressurized MDI), as seen in the image below:

Pressurized metered-dose inhalers: Drugs are propelled from a canister in the pMDI with the aid of a propellant. These devices are convenient, portable, and typically deliver 50–200 doses of the drug.

Dry powder inhalers: Drugs may also be delivered as a dry powder using devices that scatter a fine powder dispersed by air turbulence on inhalation. Children less than 7 years of age find it difficult to use a DPI. DPIs have been developed to deliver peptides and proteins, such as insulin, systemically but have proved to be problematic because of the consistency of dosing.

The given image shows various types of dry powder inhalers:

Nebulizers: Two types of nebulizers are available. Jet nebulizers are driven by a stream of gas (air or oxygen), whereas ultrasonic nebulizers use a rapidly vibrating piezoelectric crystal and thus do not require a source of compressed gas.

The nebulized drug may be inspired during tidal breathing, and it is possible to deliver much higher doses of the drug as compared to pMDI. Nebulizers are therefore useful in treating acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD, for delivering drugs when airway obstruction is extreme (e.g., in severe COPD), for delivering inhaled drugs to infants and small children who cannot use the other inhalation devices, and for giving drugs such as antibiotics when relatively high doses must be delivered.
questions.learning: Drug deposition in the oropharynx — The given image shows a metered-dose inhaler (MDI). The most common side effect of this device is drug deposition in the oropharynx.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are major criteria under the Jones Criteria for Acute Rheumatic Fever? 1. Chorea 2. Erythema marginatum 3. Subcutaneous nodules 4. Polyarthralgia Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

The five major Jones criteria are:

1. Carditis
2. Polyarthritis
3. Chorea (Sydenham's chorea)
4. Erythema marginatum
5. Subcutaneous nodules

So Chorea, Erythema marginatum, and Subcutaneous nodules are all major criteria.

Why option with Polyarthralgia is wrong: This is the key trap in the question — polyarthralgia is a minor criterion, not major. The major criterion is polyarthritis (objective joint inflammation), while polyarthralgia (joint pain without objective inflammation) only counts as minor — and importantly, if polyarthritis is already used as a major criterion, polyarthralgia cannot also be counted as a minor criterion in the same patient (to avoid double-counting the same joint symptom).

Minor criteria (for reference, high-yield alongside majors):

• Fever
• Polyarthralgia (only if polyarthritis isn't used as major)
• Elevated ESR/CRP
• Prolonged PR interval on ECG (only if carditis isn't used as major)
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 The five major Jones criteria are: 1. Subcutaneous nodules So Chorea, Erythema marginatum, and Subcutaneous nodules are all major criteria.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Three female children graphs were plotted on an IAP growth chart, which of them signals growth failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only 3

Out of the growth curves (weight-for-age), only growth curve 3 shows growth failure. This pattern shows fluctuation in growth percentiles, which might indicate a history of growth issues or inconsistent growth. The drop to below -2SD is significant and suggests growth failure as it indicates the child is significantly below the normal range.

The nutritional status of a child is assessed in terms of anthropometry:

The World Health Organization (WHO) has established international standards for normal child growth from birth to 5 years of age. The normalization of the anthropometric measures is done in terms of z-scores (standard deviation scores). The anthropometric indicators are marked in a growth chart which is compared with a reference curve.

The anthropometric measures used are weight for age, height for age, weight for height, BMI, and mid-upper arm circumference.

• Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition. It is also mentioned as wasting.
• High weight-for-height indicates overweight.
• Low height-for-age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.
• Low weight-for-age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

The below image shows the WHO growth chart for girls (6 months-2years). Boys have similar charting in blue color.
questions.learning: Only 3 Out of the growth curves (weight-for-age), only growth curve 3 shows growth failure. This pattern shows fluctuation in growth percentiles, which might indicate a history of growth issues or inconsistent growth.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Match the following part of GIT with their histologic findings: GIT: 1. Oesophagus 2. Transverse colon 3. Duodenum 4. Terminal ileum Histology: a. Taenia coli and haustrations b. Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium c. Peyer’s patches and mucus-secreting goblet cells d. Villi and submucosal glands
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

Each segment of the gastrointestinal tract has characteristic histological features that reflect its specialized function. Recognizing these hallmark findings is essential for identifying GIT sections in histology.

Correct Match:

• 1. Oesophagus → b. non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium
• 2. Transverse colon → a. Taenia coli and haustrations
• 3. Duodenum → d. Villi and submucosal (Brunner’s) glands
• 4. Terminal ileum → c. Peyer’s patches and mucus-secreting goblet cells

Why not the other options?

• Oesophagus does not have villi or Brunner’s glands.
• Colon lacks villi and Peyer’s patches; it is identified by taenia coli, haustra, and abundant goblet cells.
• Duodenum is distinguished by Brunner’s glands in the submucosa.
• Terminal ileum contains Peyer’s patches, which are aggregated lymphoid follicles.
questions.learning: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c Each segment of the gastrointestinal tract has characteristic histological features that reflect its specialized function. Recognizing these hallmark findings is essential for identifying GIT sections in histology.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young man presents with weakness affecting the lower half of the right side of his face, resulting in drooping of the angle of the mouth. He is unable to raise his eyebrows on either side. What is the most appropriate diagnosis for this presentation?
options: Infranuclear facial palsy on right side
Supranuclear facial palsy on left side
Supranuclear facial palsy on right side
questions.explanation: An infranuclear (Lower Motor Neuron) facial palsy occurs when the facial nerve (CN VII) is damaged after exiting the brainstem, causing ipsilateral paralysis of all facial muscles. This includes the lower face, resulting in mouth drooping, and the upper face, preventing the patient from raising their eyebrow or closing their eye on the affected side. In contrast, a supranuclear (Upper Motor Neuron) lesion (Options B and D) spares the forehead muscles due to bilateral cortical innervation of the upper facial nucleus; only the contralateral lower face would be weak. Since this patient has drooping on the right side and cannot raise the right eyebrow (part of "both sides" mentioned in clinical signs), it confirms a right-sided infranuclear lesion. Left-sided palsy (Option C) is ruled out as the symptoms are on the right
questions.learning: An infranuclear (Lower Motor Neuron) facial palsy occurs when the facial nerve (CN VII) is damaged after exiting the brainstem, causing ipsilateral paralysis of all facial muscles.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Most effective antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced vomiting is_________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Granisetron

Among the given options, the most effective antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced vomiting is granisetron.

Granisetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist. They are the most effective drugs for the treatment of chemotherapy-induced and post-operative nausea and vomiting.

Palonosetron is a second-generation 5HT3 antagonist that has the highest affinity for 5HT3 receptors and has the maximum potency. It is also the longest acting that makes it effective in delayed emesis associated with chemotherapy. Palonosetron has minimal/no propensity to cause QT interval prolongation.
questions.learning: Granisetron Among the given options, the most effective antiemetic for chemotherapy-induced vomiting is granisetron. Granisetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: How should steroid therapy be administered for a 55-year-old male diagnosed with Addison's disease?
options: Bolus of 100mg, followed by 200mg over 24 hours
Bolus of 200 mg, followed by 500 mg over 24 hours
questions.explanation: In the management of an Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), rapid replacement of glucocorticoids is life-saving. The standard protocol involves an immediate intravenous bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone. This is followed by either continuous infusion or intermittent doses totaling 200 mg over the subsequent 24 hours. Options C and D (500 mg) represent excessively high doses that are generally not required and increase the risk of side effects. Hydrocortisone is preferred because it has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, though aggressive fluid resuscitation with normal saline is also mandatory to correct the associated hypotension and electrolyte imbalances (hyponatremia/hyperkalemia). Once the patient is stabilized and can tolerate oral intake, the dose is gradually tapered to a maintenance level (typically 15–25 mg daily). Identifying the trigger for the crisis, such as infection or stress, is also a critical part of management to prevent future life-threatening episodes
questions.learning: In the management of an Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), rapid replacement of glucocorticoids is life-saving. The standard protocol involves an immediate intravenous bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 36-year-old farmer came to the clinic with cough, chest pain for one week, and fatigue for a month, and his Chest X-ray was taken which is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydatid cyst

The chronic history, the frequent exposure to animals as he is a farmer, and the chest x-ray which shows a cystic lesion in the right lung are suggestive of Hydatid disease.

* The causative organism of hydatid disease is Echinococcus granulosus and it belongs to the class cestodes.

* It is a tape-like, segmented worm. It infects man accidentally, giving rise to hydatid cysts.

* Dogs are the definitive hosts of E. granulosus.

* Sheep are the usual intermediate hosts, but humans are accidental intermediate hosts. Humans are end-stage hosts of the parasite since there is no human to human transmission

The hydatid cyst wall consists of 3 layers:

* Pericyst- the outer dense fibrous capsule that is formed as a result of host inflammatory response.

* Ectocyst- the intermediate layer consisting of acellular, chitinous, laminated hyaline material.

* Endocyst- the inner germinal layer that is cellular and consists of a number of nuclei embedded in protoplasmic mass and is extremely thin. It is the vital layer of the cyst and it is the site of asexual reproduction giving rise to brood capsules with scolices.

The clinical features of hydatid disease of the lung are breathlessness, cough, hemoptysis, and chest pain.

Treatment includes wedge resection or lobectomy and administration of albendazole.

Other options:

* Asbestosis presents as pleural plaques, irregular opacities, ground-glass appearance particularly present at the lower lung fields. HRCT will show the presence of pleural plaque, subpleural curvilinear lines 5–10 mm in length that appears to be parallel to the pleura.

* Silicosis is an occupational disease and is caused by exposure to silica. It is seen in people who work in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, and quarrying. It presents as small rounded opacities in the upper lobe. There may be calcification of hilar lymph nodes which leads to the appearance of eggshell calcification. HRCT will show a characteristic crazy paving pattern.

* Byssinosis is an occupational disease due to chronic exposure to cotton dust as in yarns of textile and rope-making industries. In the early stage of the disease, patients complain of occasional chest tightness towards the end of the first day of the workweek termed as monday chest tightness. As the day progress, the chest tightness may recur or persist throughout the week. Chest X-ray shows hyperlucency, diaphragmatic flattening, and emphysema. A chest CT demonstrates ground glass opacities largely distributed in then basal fashion with centrilobular nodules.

Pearl PF1538: Indications and contraindications of puncture, aspiration, injection, and re-aspiration (PAIR) in hydatid cyst

Indications:

* Relapse cyst, infected cyst, cyst >5 cm in different liver segments

* Patients who refuse surgery or where surgery is contraindicated

* Pregnant women, children < 3 years of age

* WHO - type CE1 and type CE3a.

Contraindications:

* Cysts in lung

* Cysts communicating with bile duct

* Cysts with multiple septae—honeycomb cysts

* Inaccessible cysts

* Hyperechogenic cysts

* Calcified cysts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who underwent Nissen's fundoplication was seen in the ward during evening rounds. He is asymptomatic at present with stable vitals. What is the next line of management for this patient?
options: Nasogastric tube to prevent gas bloat syndrome
Insert chest tube to prevent pneumothorax
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Monitor vitals

The patient is asymptomatic, therefore no further action needs to be taken other than monitoring his vitals.

The most common complication of Nissen’s fundoplication is gas-bloat syndrome.

Fundoplication is a procedure in which the fundus of the stomach is wrapped around the lower end of the esophagus. After this procedure, most patients are unable to belch gas from the stomach into the esophagus. This causes increased gas in the stomach resulting in bloating sensation, abdominal discomfort, and flatulence. This is known as gas bloat syndrome and occurs more commonly with Nissen total fundoplication.

Other options:

During the early postoperative period, patients who report persistent nausea and demonstrate inadequate intake of a liquid diet should undergo abdominal radiography. If significant gastric distention is identified, a nasogastric tube can safely be placed to decompress the stomach for 24 hours.

Pneumothorax is the most common complication that occurs intraoperatively. Chest tube needs to be inserted if pneumothorax takes place, which is not seen in this case.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During a modified radical neck dissection, which of the following anatomical structures is not preserved?
questions.explanation: Neck dissections are performed to remove lymph nodes involved in head and neck cancers. A modified radical neck dissection (MRND) is defined by the removal of all lymph node levels (I-V) while preserving one or more of the non-lymphatic structures typically removed in a "radical" dissection. These structures include the Sternocleidomastoid muscle (Option A), the Internal jugular vein (Option B), and the Spinal accessory nerve (Option C). However, the submandibular gland (found in Level Ib) is routinely excised during MRND because it is intimately associated with the Level I lymph nodes, and its preservation would compromise the oncological thoroughness of the procedure. Preserving the spinal accessory nerve is particularly crucial to avoid "shoulder syndrome," characterized by pain and limited abduction. MRND aims to achieve a balance between effective cancer control and minimizing functional morbidity. Distinguishing between radical, modified radical, and selective neck dissections is a core requirement for surgical oncology and ENT clinical practice

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What are the contraindications for the use of ventouse (vacuum extraction) during delivery?
questions.explanation: Vacuum extraction (ventouse) is contraindicated in preterm infants, generally defined as less than 34 weeks of gestation. This is because the preterm fetal head is soft and the scalp is more fragile, significantly increasing the risk of intracranial hemorrhage and subgaleal hematoma from the suction pressure. Heart disease (Option B) and decreased bear-down efforts (Option A) are actually indications for instrumental delivery (forceps or vacuum) to shorten the second stage of labor and reduce maternal effort. Dilatation (Option D) is not a contraindication; however, for any instrumental delivery, the cervix must be fully dilated . If the cervix is not fully dilated, an instrumental attempt is contraindicated. Other contraindications for ventouse include fetal face presentation and suspected fetal bleeding disorders. Consequently, prematurity stands out as a major relative contraindication due to fetal vulnerability

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with a left-to-right shunt and high-output cardiac failure. The following is his MRA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vein of Galen malformation

The MR-Angiography shown is of Vein of Galen Malformation.

Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations (VGAM's), also known as median prosencephalic arteriovenous fistula, are uncommon intracranial anomalies that tend to present in early childhood with features of a left-to-right shunt and high-output cardiac failure.

The vein of Galen, also known as the great cerebral vein or great vein of Galen, is a short trunk formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins and basal veins of Rosenthal. It lies in the quadrigeminal cistern. It curves backwards and upward around the posterior border of the splenium of the corpus callosum and drains the anterior and central regions of the brain into the sinuses of the posterior cerebral fossa.
