questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with guttate lesions in one eye and bullous keratopathy in the other eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy

Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is a progressive disorder of the corneal endothelium characterized by guttata formation and eventual stromal and epithelial edema leading to bullous keratopathy.

Key clinical progression:

• Early stage:

• Guttate lesions (corneal guttata) on Descemet’s membrane

• Late stage:

• Endothelial failure → corneal edema
• Formation of bullae (bullous keratopathy) → pain, decreased vision

Pathophysiology:

• Loss of endothelial cells → impaired corneal deturgescence (fluid pump function)
• Leads to fluid accumulation in cornea

Why not others:

• Interstitial keratitis: Stromal inflammation, not endothelial dystrophy
• Viral corneal ulcer: Epithelial defect, dendritic pattern
• Keratoconjunctivitis: Surface inflammation, no guttata

A 4 hour wait is recommended before intervention when the active phase is slow.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Mark the correct statement/s about Inner and Outer hair cells. 1. Inner hair cells are in a single row and transmit auditory impulses. 2. Outer hair cells are in 3-4 rows and modulate function of inner hair cells. 3. Outer hair cells are more responsible for movement of tectorial membrane. 4. Inner hair cells are in single row and modulate function of outer hair cells. 5. Outer and inner hair cells are present in the ratio 3:1.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 5 are correct

Understanding the structure and function of inner and outer hair cells in the organ of Corti is essential for interpreting hearing physiology.

OHC : IHC = \~3 : 1

Inner Hair Cells (IHC):

• Arranged in single row
• Primary sensory receptors
• Transmit auditory impulses to brain via afferent fibers

Outer Hair Cells (OHC):

• Arranged in 3–4 rows
• Function: modulation and amplification of sound
• Show electromotility (prestin protein) → enhance basilar membrane vibration
• Help in fine-tuning frequency and sensitivity

Incorrect statements explained:

• Statement 3: OHC do not primarily move the tectorial membrane; they amplify basilar membrane motion
• Statement 4: IHC do NOT modulate OHC; rather OHC modulate IHC function
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 5 are correct Understanding the structure and function of inner and outer hair cells in the organ of Corti is essential for interpreting hearing physiology.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young boy is brought for developmental evaluation. On examination, he has prominent epicanthal folds, a single transverse palmar crease, hypotonia, intellectual disability, a flat facial profile, and upslanting palpebral fissures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Down syndrome, caused by trisomy 21, is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. Its characteristic physical findings include a flat facial profile, prominent epicanthal folds, and upslanting palpebral fissures. Hand examination frequently reveals a single transverse palmar (simian) crease and hypotonia. Patau syndrome (Option B) presents with trisomy 13 features like cleft lip and polydactyly. Edward syndrome (Option C) features include clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet due to trisomy 18. Fragile X syndrome (Option D) involves a long, narrow face and large ears but lacks the specific palmar crease and facial features of Down syndrome. Therefore, the described constellation of findings is pathognomonic for trisomy 21
questions.learning: Down syndrome, caused by trisomy 21, is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. Its characteristic physical findings include a flat facial profile, prominent epicanthal folds, and upslanting palpebral fissures.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with intermittent jaundice and splenomegaly. There is a history of similar complaints in the elder brother. Peripheral smear shows the following finding. How will you investigate this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Osmotic fragility test - Hereditary spherocytosis

The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical condition and the peripheral smear showing spherocytes is hereditary spherocytosis. The investigation that can be done in this condition is the osmotic fragility test.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is mostly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The mutations commonly affect ankyrin, band 3, spectrin, or band 4.2.

This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice, anemia, and splenomegaly. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones in early adulthood. Pigment stones are found in 40-50% of the affected adults.

Laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor.

Laboratory investigations that are done to confirm the diagnosis:

• Osmotic fragility test
• Acid glycerol lysis test
• Eosin-5’-maleimide (EMA)–binding test
• SDS-gel electrophoresis test

There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy.

Other Options:

Option B: Coombs test - AIHA (Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia) - This test is performed to determine if the patient's red blood cells are coated with immunoglobulins or complement, leading to their destruction. AIHA typically does not present with a family history.

Option C: G6PD deficiency - This condition is characterized by hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stress, such as infections or exposure to certain drugs. G6PD deficiency is diagnosed by measuring G6PD enzyme activity or genetic testing.

Option D: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria - This rare acquired hemolytic anemia is characterized by episodes of hemolysis and hemoglobinuria, particularly during sleep. The diagnosis is made by testing for the presence of GPI-anchored proteins using flow cytometry.
questions.learning: Osmotic fragility test - Hereditary spherocytosis — The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical condition and the peripheral smear showing spherocytes is hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which oxygen delivery device provides a fixed and consistent FiO₂ of 0.25–0.60, independent of the patient’s respiratory pattern?
questions.explanation: Oxygen delivery systems are classified as low-flow or high-flow. The Venturi mask (Option C) is a high-flow system that utilizes the Bernoulli principle to mix a specific flow of oxygen with room air. This creates a fixed, accurate fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) typically ranging from 0.24 to 0.60, which remains constant regardless of the patient's inspiratory flow rate or depth of breathing. Nasal cannulae (Option A) and simple face masks (Option B) are low-flow systems where the actual FiO2 varies significantly based on the patient's respiratory effort and room air entrainment. A non-rebreathing mask (Option D) provides high FiO2 (up to 0.90) but is also a reservoir-dependent system that does not offer the same precise titration as a Venturi mask. Therefore, the Venturi mask is the most reliable system for patients requiring a precise, constant oxygen concentration, such as those with COPD
questions.learning: Oxygen delivery systems are classified as low-flow or high-flow. The Venturi mask (Option C) is a high-flow system that utilizes the Bernoulli principle to mix a specific flow of oxygen with room air.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Most common site of ossifying fibroma is?
questions.explanation: An ossifying fibroma is a benign but locally aggressive fibro-osseous lesion. It is characterized by the replacement of normal bone with a combination of fibrous tissue and mineralized material. Statistically, the mandible is the most common site of occurrence, specifically in the premolar and molar regions. While it can occur in the maxilla (Option B) or paranasal sinuses like the frontal (Option A) or maxillary sinus (Option D), these locations are less frequent than the lower jaw. Ossifying fibromas typically present as a painless, slowly enlarging hard swelling that can cause facial asymmetry or tooth displacement. On imaging, they appear as a well-demarcated lesion with varying degrees of radiopacity depending on the amount of calcified tissue present. Therefore, Mandible is the correct anatomical site recognized as the most frequent location for this tumor
questions.learning: An ossifying fibroma is a benign but locally aggressive fibro-osseous lesion. It is characterized by the replacement of normal bone with a combination of fibrous tissue and mineralized material.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Glands of Cloquet are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphatic drainage of vulva

The Gland (Node) of Cloquet, also known as the Rosenmüller node, is the highest deep inguinal lymph node, located in the femoral canal beneath the inguinal ligament. It serves as a link between the deep inguinal lymph nodes and the external iliac lymph nodes and is an important sentinel node in the lymphatic drainage of the vulva.

• The vulva drains primarily to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, then to the deep inguinal nodes, including the Node of Cloquet, before reaching the external iliac nodes.
• It is clinically important in carcinoma of the vulva, as involvement of the Node of Cloquet suggests more advanced nodal spread.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lymphatic drainage of cervix: The cervix drains mainly to the parametrial, obturator, internal iliac, external iliac, and sacral lymph nodes.
• C. Lymphatic drainage of uterus: The uterus drains to the external iliac, internal iliac, para-aortic (lumbar), and superficial inguinal nodes (via the round ligament from the fundus).
• D. Lubricating glands of vagina: Vaginal lubrication is provided mainly by Bartholin’s glands (greater vestibular glands) and cervical secretions. There are no glands within the vaginal mucosa.
questions.learning: Lymphatic drainage of vulva — The Gland (Node) of Cloquet, also known as the Rosenmüller node, is the highest deep inguinal lymph node, located in the femoral canal beneath the inguinal ligament.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is associated with the Curtain falling sign?
questions.explanation: The "curtain falling" sign (or curtain-like loss of vision) is a classic symptom of retinal detachment. As the retina peels away from the underlying pigment epithelium, the patient perceives a dark shadow or "curtain" descending over their field of vision. This is often preceded by flashes of light (photopsia) and a sudden onset of "floaters". Macular degeneration (Option B) causes a gradual loss of central vision rather than a sudden peripheral "curtain". Optic atrophy (Option C) involves the death of the optic nerve fibers and typically results in a slow, progressive decline in vision and color perception. Acute anterior uveitis (Option D) presents with a painful, red eye and photophobia, but not the specific curtain-like visual field loss. Sudden painless vision loss described as a curtain that resolves quickly is known as amaurosis fugax, which is often a precursor to a stroke. However, in a persistent state, it remains a hallmark of retinal detachment, which requires urgent surgical repair
questions.learning: The "curtain falling" sign (or curtain-like loss of vision) is a classic symptom of retinal detachment. As the retina peels away from the underlying pigment epithelium, the patient perceives a dark shadow or "curtain" descending over their field of vision.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In urea cycle disorders, which of the following can be used to reduce the levels of ammonia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phenylbutyrate

Phenylbutyrate can be used to reduce ammonia levels in patients with urea cycle disorders.

Phenylbutyrate diverts urea into an alternate pathway and reduces the amount of ammonia. Hence, acting as an ammonia scavenger. Other drugs that can be used to achieve the same outcome (ammonia scavengers) include phenylacetate and benzoate.

Note: Arginine is used as first-line treatment as it provides ornithine; a positive regulator of the urea cycle. Arginine also activates NAG synthase which increases NAG; a positive regulator of the urea cycle
questions.learning: Phenylbutyrate Phenylbutyrate can be used to reduce ammonia levels in patients with urea cycle disorders. Phenylbutyrate diverts urea into an alternate pathway and reduces the amount of ammonia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about laryngomalacia?
options: Patient will present with an inspiratory stridor.
It is the most common congenital cause of stridor in children.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stridor improves in supine position.

In laryngomalacia, stridor improves in prone position.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital cause of stridor. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis.  It presents just after birth and subsides by 2 years of age. Stridor is increased on crying but improves (decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding. The cry is normal.

Direct laryngoscopy shows -

* Elongated epiglottis, curled upon itself (omega-shaped)

* Floppy aryepiglottic folds, and

* Prominent arytenoids

A flexible laryngoscope is very useful to make the diagnosis. Laryngomalacia cannot be visualized in a paralyzed patient.

The below image shows the omega-shaped epiglottis:

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both

* Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:

* Mostly, it self corrects by 2 years of age.

* Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.

* Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

Important differentials:

Condition
Findings

Croup

Non-toxic, viral prodrome, barking cough

X-ray neck shows steeple sign

Epiglottitis

Toxic child, drooling saliva

Lateral X-ray neck shows thumb sign

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is on antidiabetic medications and telmisartan. Her HbA1c is 8.5%. Her blood pressure is well controlled, eGFR is 50 mL/min/1.73 m², serum potassium is normal, and she is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate intervention to reduce the risk of further decline in eGFR?
options: Increase the dose of anti-diabetic drug
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase the dose of telmisartan

Maximizing renin–angiotensin system (RAS) blockade with an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the cornerstone of slowing the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD). In patients with hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease, the ARB dose should be titrated to the maximum tolerated dose to reduce intraglomerular pressure, proteinuria, and the rate of eGFR decline, provided serum creatinine and potassium remain acceptable.

Why not the other options?

• B. Shift to ramipril: ACE inhibitors and ARBs provide comparable renal protection. Switching from a well-tolerated ARB to an ACE inhibitor offers no additional benefit.
• C. Increase the dose of anti-diabetic drug: Better glycemic control is important, but optimizing RAS blockade has a more direct renoprotective effect in diabetic kidney disease.
• D. Start carvedilol: Useful for hypertension or heart failure but does not specifically reduce the progression of diabetic kidney disease.
questions.learning: Increase the dose of telmisartan Maximizing renin–angiotensin system (RAS) blockade with an ACE inhibitor or ARB is the cornerstone of slowing the progression of diabetic kidney disease (DKD).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a non-parametric test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Friedman test

Friedman test is a non-parametric test. It is used to test for differences between groups when the dependent variable being measured is ordinal.

Other options:

Student t-test, analysis of variation (ANOVA) test, and pearson correlation are all based on quantitative data and hence grouped under parametric tests.
questions.learning: Friedman test Friedman test is a non-parametric test. It is used to test for differences between groups when the dependent variable being measured is ordinal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Certain new vaccines are being studied in the market and their efficacies are compared and presented in the image as shown below. Which of the newer vaccines can be used with the same efficacy as compared to the previous vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C, D and E

Vaccines C, D, and E can be used with the same efficacy as compared to the previous vaccine, as their confidence interval lies within the zone of equivalence.

In a classical randomized controlled trial (RCT), the aim is to evaluate a difference between two drugs by proving the superiority of the new drug over the standard drug. However, an equivalence study is carried out with the aim of showing there are no significant differences in the efficacy between the new drug and the standard drug.

To define 'no significant differences' the limit of equivalence (δ) must be defined first. δ must be set as superiority margin (+δ) and non-inferiority margin (-δ), so that they are clinically appropriate and the differences can be tolerated as clinically irrelevant. To conclude equivalence the confidence interval (CI), i.e., the whisker (tail) of the box-whisker plot must lie within the zone of equivalence.

Therefore in the given question, vaccines C, D, and E have CI in the zone of equivalence and thus have the same efficacy as the previous vaccine. Vaccines F and G lie outside the zone of equivalence but well within +δ, making them superior to the previous vaccine. Vaccines A and B lie outside the zone of equivalence but well within -δ, making them non-equivalent and at the same time non-inferior to the previous vaccine. If the CI of any vaccine includes or crosses the -δ limit, they will be considered inferior to the standard vaccine.

Note: A superiority trial is done to show that the new drug is superior to the standard drug. A non-inferiority trial is done to show that the new drug is not worse than the standard drug. This is done for newer interventions or drugs that may be less costly, less invasive, and have fewer side effects.
questions.learning: C, D and E Vaccines C, D, and E can be used with the same efficacy as compared to the previous vaccine, as their confidence interval lies within the zone of equivalence.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male professional trumpet player presents with a swelling on the left side of the neck that produces a gurgling sound on compression. An X-ray of the neck demonstrates characteristic findings. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A laryngocele is an abnormal cystic expansion of the laryngeal saccule. The patient’s profession as a trumpet player is a classic risk factor because increased endolaryngeal pressure can force air into the saccule, causing it to dilate. The clinical sign of a "gurgling sound" or the sac emptying upon compression (Bryce’s sign) is highly suggestive. The provided X-ray confirms the diagnosis by showing a clear, air-filled radiolucent space in the neck. Option A (Pharyngeal pouch) is located lower in the neck and usually contains food/fluid rather than just air. Option C (Trachea-oesophageal fistula) presents with coughing and aspiration during feeding, not as a compressible neck mass. Option D (Tonsillar cyst) is a small, superficial lesion within the oropharynx. Laryngoceles can become infected or cause airway obstruction. They are also associated with laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, which can obstruct the saccule opening. Surgical management is indicated for symptomatic or large lesions
questions.learning: A laryngocele is an abnormal cystic expansion of the laryngeal saccule. The patient’s profession as a trumpet player is a classic risk factor because increased endolaryngeal pressure can force air into the saccule, causing it to dilate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 17-year-old woman with no comorbidities presents with numbness and paraesthesia of the fingers along with the characteristic finding as shown in the image below. She has no history of smoking or history of other illnesses. She mentions the episodes occur when she is under excess stress or during cold temperatures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Raynaud's phenomenon

The image along with the history of no previous illness in a young female is most likely of Raynaud's phenomenon.

Raynaud's phenomenon:

* Episodic digital ischemia due to the vasospasm of digital arteries.

* Cold exposure or emotional stress can trigger it.

* The blanching/ischemic phase of the phenomenon with pallor/cyanosis is often accompanied by numbness and paraesthesia.

* Capillaries and venules dilate and cyanosis results from the deoxygenated blood that is present in these vessels.

* Color changes are usually well-demarcated and are confined to the fingers or toes.

* In the rewarming phase, digital vasospasm resolves and blood flows into the dilated arterioles and capillaries increase dramatically causing reactive hyperemia which imparts bright red color to the digits.

* Some may experience only pallor cyanosis while others experience both pallor and cyanosis.

Types of Raynaud's:
1.Primary/idiopathic

2. Secondary associated with other diseases like:

* Collagen vascular diseases: scleroderma, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, dermatomyositis, polymyositis

* Arterial occlusive diseases: atherosclerosis of the extremities, thromboangiitis
obliterans, acute arterial occlusion

* Neurologic disorders: intervertebral disk disease, syringomyelia

* Blood dyscrasias: cold agglutinins, cryoglobulinemia, cryofibrinogenemia,

* Trauma: vibration injury, electric shock, cold injury, typing, piano playing

* Drugs and toxins: ergot derivatives, methysergide, β-adrenergic receptor
blockers

Management:

* Reassurance, warm clothing, and avoiding cold exposures.
exposure.

* Reduce or abstain from smoking and reduce stress levels.

* Drug treatments such as CCB's(nifedipine, amlodipine), alpha 1 blockers ( prazosin) are used only for advanced cases.

* In secondary Raynauds's Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors like sildenafil, tadalafil may improve symptoms.

Other options:

Buerger's disease or thromboangiitis obliterans involves occlusive disease of small- and medium-sized arteries, thrombophlebitis of the superficial or deep veins, and Raynaud’s syndrome. It occurs in male smokers, usually under the age of 30 years. It is an arterial occlusive disorder, so compression stockings will have no therapeutic effect.

Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) presents as intermittent claudication, which is pain that increases with walking and may sometimes present with rest pain. It is generally caused by atherosclerosis but may also be due to trauma. The initial investigation done is an ABPI. Physical exam findings include atrophied skin, pallor on raising leg (Buerger's test), nail changes, and decreased peripheral pulses.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Sickness absenteeism of workers in the industry is used to evaluate__________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Health of the worker

Sickness absenteeism of workers in the industry is used to evaluate the health of the workers.

Sickness absenteeism refers to employees' self-reported absence from work due to health problems. The apparent cause for sickness absenteeism may or may not be due to actual sickness. These include

* Economic causes: reporting sick to avail a sick leave with pay

* Social causes: obligations such as weddings, and festivals

* Medical causes: due to occupational accidents

* Non-occupational causes: nutritional disorders, alcoholism and drug addiction.

Absenteeism is an index used in industries to assess the state of health of workers and their physical, mental and social well-being. Interventions to reduce sickness absenteeism should focus on areas, such as periodic medical checkups, monitoring work schedules, improving employees’ job satisfaction, and reducing workplace stress.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na+K+ATPase results in __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Depolarisation

The inhibition of Na+K+-ATPase results in depolarisation.

An energy (ATP)-dependent pump system (Na+/K+-ATPase), is located on the sarcolemma, which pumps Na+ out and K+ into the cell.The Na+/K+-ATPase pump is electrogenic because it extrudes three Na+ for every two K+ entering the cell. By pumping more positive charges out of the cell than into it, the pump creates a negative potential within the cell. This electrogenic potential may be up to −10 mV.

If this pump stops working (such as when ATP is lost under hypoxic conditions), or if the activity of the pump is inhibited by cardiac glycosides such as digoxin, Na+ accumulates within the cell and intracellular K+ falls,resulting in a less negative (more depolarized) resting membrane potential.

Inhibition of this pump, therefore, causes depolarization resulting from changes in Na+ and K+ concentration gradients and from the loss of an electrogenic component of the membrane potential.

Action potential of myocardium:

* Phase 0: Depolarisation: Influx of Na+ into myocyte.

* Phase 1: Early repolarization: Efflux of K+ from myocyte.

* Phase 2: Plateau: Ca2+ enters myocardial cells via voltage regulated L-type Ca2+ channels.

* Phase 3: Repolarisation: Efflux of K+.

* Phase 4: Restoration of RMP: Restoration of Na+ and K+ by Na-K ATPase.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presented with difficulty in hearing. A pure-tone audiogram was obtained, which is shown below. What is the interpretation of this audiogram?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left-sided mixed hearing loss

The given audiogram is suggestive of left-sided mixed hearing loss.

Interpretation of the audiogram:

* Blue colour indicates the left ear.

* > indicates bone conduction (BC), and the threshold is >25 dB. Hence, BC is abnormal, which implies that the abnormality is in the sensorineural pathway.

* × indicates air conduction (AC), and the threshold is >15 dB. Hence, AC is abnormal.

* Both AC and BC are abnormal. It indicates sensorineural hearing loss.

* In addition, the air-bone gap is present, which implies conductive hearing loss.

* Hence, the interpretation is left-mixed hearing loss.

A mixed type of hearing loss presents with defects in both conductive and sensorineural pathways. This type of hearing loss is seen in chronic suppurative otitis media and otosclerosis.
questions.learning: Left-sided mixed hearing loss — The given audiogram is suggestive of left-sided mixed hearing loss. Interpretation of the audiogram: * Blue colour indicates the left ear. * > indicates bone conduction (BC), and the threshold is >25 dB.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A gym owner noticed that people who come to the gym also drink iced tea. He concluded that drinking iced tea is the sole reason to lose weight. What is this relationship called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spurious

In the gym owner's case, concluding that iced tea alone causes weight loss is a spurious relationship because it ignores other key factors like exercise and overall diet.

A spurious relationship is when two variables appear to be connected but are actually linked by another factor or are coincidental. In this scenario, the gym owner observed that gym-goers also drink iced tea and concluded that iced tea is the sole cause of weight loss. However, this conclusion is just coincidental because it ignores other important factors, such as exercise, diet, and lifestyle changes, which likely contribute to weight loss.

An association can be broadly grouped under three headings:

* Spurious association

* Indirect association

* Direct (causal) association: One-to-one causal association and Multifactorial causation

Option B: Direct (causal) association: Two variables are stated to be causally related (AB) if a change in A is followed by a change in B. When factor A is present, disease B must result. Measles is one such disease in which such a relation exists.

Option C: Indirect association: The indirect association is an association between a variable and disease due to the presence of another factor, known or unknown, that is also known as the "confounding" variable. For example, endemic goitre is generally found in high altitudes, thereby showing an association between altitude and endemic goitre. But, endemic goitre is not due to altitude but due to an environmental deficiency of iodine. Thus, a common factor (i.e., iodine deficiency) can result in an apparent association between two variables, when no association exists.

Option D: Multifactorial causation is seen in non-communicable diseases or conditions (e.g., Coronary heart disease) where the etiology is multifactorial.
questions.learning: Spurious — In the gym owner's case, concluding that iced tea alone causes weight loss is a spurious relationship because it ignores other key factors like exercise and overall diet.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
A patient presents to the casualty following blunt trauma to the chest. A chest X-ray was done. Among the following radiographs, in which case would you further evaluate the patient before putting a chest tube?

1. Diaphragmatic hernia
2. Hemothorax
3. Pneumothorax
4. Flail chest
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1

Among the following radiographs, image 1 shows dilated bowel loops in the hemithorax, and is suggestive of diaphragmatic hernia and it needs to be evaluated further before putting a chest tube since it can cause injury to the intestinal contents in the thorax.

Blunt injury to the diaphragm can lead to rupture and therefore the abdominal contents can herniate into the chest. Nasogastric tube placement followed by chest radiography can be useful in case of herniation of the stomach into the chest. The most accurate investigation is video-assisted thoracoscopy or laparoscopy.

Operative repair should be done. Repair should be done via the abdomen in case of a diaphragmatic rupture.

Radiographs 2,3,4 are hemothorax, pneumothorax, and flail chest respectively. These conditions are life-threatening. Hence, the diagnosis and management have to be immediate. Rapid insertion of intercostal chest drains should be done. They are inserted into the fifth intercostal space. The safe landmark is identified as a triangle that lies anterior to the midaxillary line above the nipple, below, and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

The below images show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

Hemothorax can occur following blunt trauma. It occurs due to bleeding from the intercostal vessels or internal mammary artery secondary to rib fracture. Features include hemorrhagic shock, flat neck veins, unilateral absence of breath sounds, and dullness on percussion. Correction of hypovolemic shock, intercostal drain insertion, and intubation are useful in management.

Pneumothorax can be open or tension pneumothorax. In tension pneumothorax, the common etiology is penetrating or blunt trauma, and features such as tachypnea, dyspnea, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation, hyper resonance and decreased breath sounds are seen. Immediate decompression can be attained by large bore cannula insertion into the second intercostal space on the affected side in the midclavicular line after which a chest tube can be placed in the 5th intercostal space along the anterior axillary line. Chest radiograph shows mediastinal shift to the opposite side and diaphragmatic depression on the same side.

Flail chest occurs as a result of blunt trauma and is associated with rib fractures. Clinically, paradoxical movement of the chest can be present. Management includes oxygen administration, analgesia, chest drain, and surgery to stabilize the flail segment. Rib fractures can be seen on chest radiograph.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man with a recent travel history to Assam presents with fever, chills, seizures, altered sensorium, and severe hypotension (BP 70/50 mm Hg). Peripheral smear confirms Plasmodium falciparum infection. In this clinical scenario, which drug is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with "Severe Cerebral Malaria," defined by the presence of Plasmodium falciparum and neurological complications (seizures, altered sensorium) or shock (BP 70/50). According to current WHO and national guidelines, "intravenous Artesunate" is the absolute drug of choice for all cases of severe malaria in both adults and children. It is superior to quinine because it clears parasites faster and is easier to administer. Chloroquine (Option A) is no longer used for falciparum malaria due to widespread resistance. Quinine (Option B) was previously the standard but is now a second-line alternative if artesunate is unavailable, as it requires careful cardiac monitoring. Artemether (Option D) is an artemisinin derivative but is preferred in its intramuscular form only when IV access is impossible. In a comatose patient with low blood pressure, rapid parasiticidal action with IV Artesunate is life-saving
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with "Severe Cerebral Malaria," defined by the presence of Plasmodium falciparum and neurological complications (seizures, altered sensorium) or shock (BP 70/50).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In asterixis, which of the following would commonly be seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypercarbia

In asterixis, the condition commonly seen is hypercarbia. Asterixis is frequently observed in patients with hypercarbia, especially in the setting of respiratory failure or COPD, due to its effects on the central nervous system. Therefore, hypercarbia is the most appropriate option among the choices provided.

Other options:

Hypoxia refers to a condition in which there is a deficiency of oxygen reaching the tissues. While hypoxia can lead to various neurological manifestations, asterixis is not typically associated with hypoxia. Asterixis is more commonly observed in conditions affecting the central nervous system or metabolic disturbances.

Thyrotoxicosis is a condition characterized by excessive thyroid hormone levels in the bloodstream, often due to an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism). Asterixis is not a characteristic feature of thyrotoxicosis. Instead, thyrotoxicosis may present with symptoms such as palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, and tremors.

Anxiety neurosis, or anxiety disorder, refers to a group of mental health disorders characterized by excessive worry, fear, and nervousness. Asterixis is not typically associated with anxiety neurosis. While anxiety disorders can manifest with various physical symptoms, asterixis is more commonly observed in neurological or metabolic conditions.
questions.learning: Hypercarbia — In asterixis, the condition commonly seen is hypercarbia. Asterixis is frequently observed in patients with hypercarbia, especially in the setting of respiratory failure or COPD, due to its effects on the central nervous system.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a diagnosed fracture is referred to a higher center. On examination, the forearm pulses are not palpable. Based on the X-ray of the upper arm shown, which artery is most likely to have been injured?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, which is a common pediatric elbow injury. In this type of fracture, the sharp edge of the proximal bone fragment is frequently displaced anteriorly, where it can easily compress or lacerate the brachial artery. This explains the loss of distal pulses in the forearm. If untreated, this vascular compromise can lead to Volkmann's ischemic contracture. The radial artery (Option A) and ulnar artery (Option B) are branches of the brachial artery that begin distal to the elbow; while they would lose their pulse, the primary site of injury is the parent vessel. The anterior interosseous artery (Option D) is a deeper branch and is not typically the cause of major pulse loss in this context. Management requires urgent orthopedic reduction and potentially vascular repair. Identifying the high risk to the brachial artery in supracondylar fractures is a classic and life-saving requirement in emergency medicine and orthopedics

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman (P2L2) with severe endometriosis is found to have pelvic adhesions on laparoscopy. She has a history of prior tubal ligation and adhesiolysis. What is the most appropriate management option during the current laparoscopic procedure?
options: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo- oophorectomy
questions.explanation: Total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy For a 36-year-old patient with severe, recurrent endometriosis and pelvic adhesions who has already completed her family (P2L2, tubal ligation), the gold standard for definitive treatment is a total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TH-BSO). This procedure is chosen because it removes the diseased tissue and eliminates the main source of estrogen (the ovaries), which is the primary driver of endometrial tissue growth. Observation (Option A) is inappropriate for severe, symptomatic disease. Hysterectomy alone (Option B) leaves the ovaries intact, leading to a high rate of disease recurrence. Oophorectomy alone (Option C) leaves the uterus and potentially diseased tissue behind and induces premature menopause without fully addressing the uterine pathology. Therefore, TH-BSO provides the highest probability of permanent symptom relief in women without a desire for future fertility.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is admitted with high fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered mental status. The child was recently treated for acute otitis media. Lumbar puncture shows a predominance of polymorphs, protein level is raised, sugars reduced and chlorides diminished. Otoscopic examination reveals bulging of the tympanic membrane. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate intervention to manage the underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myringotomy

In a child with acute bacterial meningitis secondary to acute otitis media, the most important immediate step is drainage of the middle ear infection. Myringotomy is the treatment of choice because it:

• Provides immediate drainage of infected middle ear pus
• Reduces bacterial load and intracranial spread
• Allows culture of middle ear pus for targeted antibiotics
• Relieves pressure from bulging tympanic membrane

Radical/modified radical mastoidectomy → indicated only if mastoiditis, abscess, or complications persist despite myringotomy + antibiotics

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A factory worker sustains burns involving 25% of his body during the course of employment and subsequently develops infections and related complications. Under the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act, which benefit is he entitled to receive?
questions.explanation: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Extended Sickness Benefit is provided to insured workers who suffer from any of 34 specified long-term diseases or severe complications from work injuries that require prolonged treatment. Since the worker's 25% burns led to chronic infections and complications, he is eligible for this benefit, which can provide paid leave for up to 2 years at a higher daily rate (140% of the standard rate). Dependants' Benefit (Option A) is only applicable if the worker dies as a result of an employment injury. Standard Sickness Benefit (Option B) is limited to 91 days in a year and is for short-term illnesses. Enhanced Sickness Benefit (Option D) is specifically for insured persons undergoing sterilization procedures (vasectomy/tubectomy). Therefore, the extended benefit is the only one designed for prolonged medical complications
questions.learning: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Extended Sickness Benefit is provided to insured workers who suffer from any of 34 specified long-term diseases or severe complications from work injuries that require prolonged treatment.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to elapid snakebite: 1. Regardless of the anatomic site of bite, walking of victim should be discouraged. 2. Pressure immobilization should be used, wherever possible. 3. Ptosis can be present after elapid bite. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Elapid snakes (e.g., cobra and krait) produce predominantly neurotoxic envenomation. First aid aims to delay venom absorption until the patient reaches a healthcare facility for anti-snake venom (ASV) and supportive care.

• Statement 1. Regardless of the anatomic site of bite, walking of victim should be discouraged: Correct. Walking or unnecessary movement should be discouraged, irrespective of the bite site, as muscle activity increases lymphatic flow and accelerates venom spread.
• Statement 2. Pressure immobilization should be used, wherever possible: Correct. Pressure immobilization technique (PIT) with splinting is recommended, wherever feasible, especially for neurotoxic (elapid) bites, to slow lymphatic spread of venom.
• Statement 3. Ptosis can be present after elapid bite: Correct. Ptosis is often the earliest clinical sign of neurotoxic envenomation and may progress to ophthalmoplegia, dysphagia, respiratory muscle paralysis, and respiratory failure.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Elapid snakes (e.g., cobra and krait) produce predominantly neurotoxic envenomation. First aid aims to delay venom absorption until the patient reaches a healthcare facility for anti-snake venom (ASV) and supportive care. • Statement 1.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: During a routine ultrasound at 28 weeks of gestation, a pregnant woman’s amniotic fluid index (AFI) measures 12.8 cm. At what point in a healthy pregnancy does the AFI typically reach its maximum?
questions.explanation: The amniotic fluid index (AFI) reflects the volume of amniotic fluid and is an important indicator of fetal well-being. In a normal pregnancy, the amount of amniotic fluid gradually increases as gestation progresses due to fetal urine production and lung secretions. AFI typically reaches its maximum around 32 weeks of gestation, after which it plateaus and then gradually decreases toward term. This decline occurs due to changes in fetal swallowing and fluid dynamics. An AFI of 12.8 cm at 28 weeks falls within the normal range (5–24 cm) and is consistent with expected physiology before the peak is reached. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 30 weeks : AFI is still increasing, not at peak (C) 36 weeks : AFI has already started declining (D) 38 weeks : Further decrease toward term

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A term newborn has not passed meconium within 48 hours of birth. Abdomen is distended, and digital rectal examination produces an explosive passage of stool and flatus. What is the gold standard investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Rectal biopsy showing presence of ganglion cells
Barium enema showing narrow distal segment
Rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells
Anorectal manometry showing absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells

Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) should be suspected in a newborn with:

• Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life
• Abdominal distension
• Bilious vomiting (may occur)
• Explosive passage of stool and flatus after digital rectal examination (squirt sign)

The gold standard for diagnosis is a rectal suction biopsy demonstrating:

• Absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses
• Hypertrophied nerve trunks
• Increased acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibers

Role of other investigations

• Contrast (barium) enema: Shows a narrow aganglionic distal segment with a dilated proximal colon (transition zone); useful as a screening investigation but not confirmatory.
• Anorectal manometry: Demonstrates absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR); useful in older infants and children but not the gold standard.
• Rectal biopsy showing presence of ganglion cells: Rules out Hirschsprung disease.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with complaints of fever for 3 days and general fatigue. On examination, splinter hemorrhages were seen. Echocardiography revealed vegetations on the valves and thus a blood culture was done. The organism in the culture was seen as cocci in chains that showed alpha hemolysis on blood agar and was resistant to optochin and bile. Which of the following bacteria is most commonly implicated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus sanguis

The clinical scenario of fever, splinter haemorrhages, and vegetations on echocardiography is suggestive of infective endocarditis. The bacteria seen as cocci with alpha hemolysis and resistant to optochin and bile are most suggestive of Streptococcus viridans and in the following options, Streptococcus sanguis is a type of viridans bacteria.

Streptococcus sanguis belong to the viridans group of streptococci and they cause subacute bacterial endocarditis.

Streptococci that show alpha hemolysis on blood agar are again classified on the basis of optochin sensitivity and bile solubility.

* Alpha hemolysis: Streptococcus pneumoniae is sensitive to optochin and is bile soluble. Viridians streptococci are resistant to optochin and are bile insoluble.

* Beta hemolysis: Group B is resistant to bacitracin and Group A is sensitive to it.

* Gamma hemolysis: Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and non-enterococcus does not.

Viridans streptococci show alpha hemolysis on blood agar and are resistant to optochin. They contain:

* Streptococci sanguis causes subacute bacterial endocarditis

* Streptococci mitis

* Streptococci mutans

* Streptococci salvarius

Other options:

Option A- Streptococcus pyogenes are beta-hemolytic and bacitracin sensitive.

Option C- Enterococcus does not show hemolysis.

Option D- Streptococcus agalacticae shows beta hemolysis and is bacitracin resistant.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Refsum disease is due to:
options: Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes
Absence of beta oxidation in peroxisomes
Absence of alpha oxidation in lysosomes
Absence of beta oxidation in lysosomes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes

Refsum disease is due to the absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes.

Refsum's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. The defective enzyme is phytanoyl CoA hydroxylase, which causes alpha oxidation of fatty acids and leads to elevated levels of phytanic acid in the blood.

Clinical features are dysmorphic facies and severe neurological symptoms such as polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, nerve deafness, ichthyosis, and cerebellar ataxia.

Restricted dietary intake of phytanic acid reduces the symptoms. Management includes avoiding sources of phytanic acid such as dairy products, meat, nuts, and green leafy vegetables.
questions.learning: Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes Refsum disease is due to the absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes. Refsum's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a patient, the hypothalamic thermostat was reset from point A to point C as shown below. Which of the following happens in stage A compared to stage B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Shivering

In the above scenario, the patient's hypothalamic thermostat has been reset from point A to a higher temperature (point C). The body responds to this change by using certain measures in stage A such as shivering.

In stage A the body activates various heat gain mechanisms to match the hypothalamic temperature setpoint. These include:

• Shivering- the shivering center is located in the posterior hypothalamus. It is normally inhibited by signals from the heat center in the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area but is excited by cold signals from the skin and spinal cord. A sudden increase in heat setpoint results in the activation of this center. It then transmits non-rhythmic signals through bilateral tracts through the lateral columns of the spinal cord, and finally to the anterior motor neurons. They increase the tone of the skeletal muscles throughout the body. As the tone rises above a certain critical level, shivering begins. During maximum shivering, body heat production can rise to four to five times normal.
• Vasoconstriction (decreased blood flow to skin) is mediated by increased sympathetic drive by the activation of the posterior hypothalamic sympathetic center.
• An increase in chemical thermogenesis in which heat production takes place in the brown fat by the mechanism of uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This is the predominant mechanism seen in neonates.

In stage B, the hypothalamic temperature setpoint is lower than the normal body temperature. Hence body activates various heat loss mechanisms to match the hypothalamic temperature setpoint. It includes vasodilatation of the skin blood vessel, sweating, and decreased thermogenesis.

The temperature of the body is regulated majorly by a nervous feedback mechanism that operates through temperature-regulating centers located in the hypothalamus. Minor regulation is done by the thermal receptors in the skin and the deep thermal receptors present in the spinal cord and abdominal viscera.
questions.learning: Shivering — In the above scenario, the patient's hypothalamic thermostat has been reset from point A to a higher temperature (point C). The body responds to this change by using certain measures in stage A such as shivering.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the disease depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation: The clinical diagram illustrates the classic phenotypic features of Cushing’s syndrome, which results from chronic exposure to excessive glucocorticoids. Key features shown include central obesity with a "pendulous abdomen," thin extremities due to muscle wasting, red cheeks (plethora), a "buffalo hump" (fat pads behind the neck), and purple abdominal stretch marks (striae) . Acromegaly (Option A) is caused by excess growth hormone and presents with enlarged hands, feet, and coarse facial features. PCOS (Option B) involves hyperandrogenism and hirsutism in women but lacks the distinct buffalo hump and thin limbs. Advanced obesity (Option D) presents with generalized fat distribution without the characteristic muscle wasting or purple striae. Diagnosis is typically confirmed via 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or low-dose dexamethasone suppression tests. The most common cause is exogenous steroid use, followed by pituitary adenomas (Cushing's disease) and ectopic ACTH production
questions.learning: The clinical diagram illustrates the classic phenotypic features of Cushing’s syndrome, which results from chronic exposure to excessive glucocorticoids.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent infections. Laboratory investigations reveal low levels of both B and T lymphocytes. Genetic testing demonstrates a mutation in the adenosine deaminase (ADA) gene. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

A mutation in adenosine deaminase (ADA) leading to low B and T lymphocytes is characteristic of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID).

• ADA deficiency → accumulation of deoxyadenosine and dATP
• These metabolites are toxic to lymphocytes
• Inhibit DNA synthesis → failure of lymphocyte proliferation

Immunological consequence:

• ↓ T cells + ↓ B cells → combined immunodeficiency
• Leads to severe, recurrent infections early in life

Clinical features:

• Recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections
• Failure to thrive
• Absent lymphoid tissue (e.g., tonsils)

Why other options are incorrect:

• X-linked agammaglobulinemia: Only B-cell deficiency
• CVID: Primarily B-cell dysfunction, later onset
• DiGeorge syndrome: T-cell deficiency due to thymic aplasia (not ADA defect)

questions.text: Which of the following is the most common end-product of fatty acid synthesis pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Palmitic acid

The most common end product of fatty acid synthesis is palmitic acid.

Palmitic acid is a 16 carbon saturated long chain fatty acid (LCFA). The substrate for its synthesis is acetyl CoA. Acetyl CoA is also the end product of fatty acid beta-oxidation.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: If a person starts to serve a second employer, the new employer is responsible for his actions by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Borrowed servant doctrine

When an employee is being borrowed, the lending employer temporarily surrenders control over this worker and the borrowing employer temporarily assumes control. This is known as borrowed servant doctrine.

Vicarious liability is by which the employer is responsible for his employees’ negligence if such activity occurs in the course of the employment and within its scope.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents with deep vein thrombosis along with a characteristic necrolytic migratory rash. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A glucagonoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreatic alpha cells that secretes excessive amounts of glucagon. This results in a clinical syndrome often referred to as the "4 Ds": Diabetes mellitus (usually mild), Dermatitis (specifically Necrolytic Migratory Erythema), DVT (thromboembolism), and Depression. Necrolytic migratory erythema (NME) is the most characteristic finding, presenting as painful or itchy erythematous plaques that blister and crust, typically starting in the groin or perineum and spreading. The excess glucagon drives hyperglycemia and a catabolic state, leading to weight loss and anemia. Insulinoma (Option A) causes hypoglycemia. Gastrinoma (Option B) causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with severe peptic ulcers. VIPoma (Option D) leads to Verner-Morrison syndrome, characterized by "pancreatic cholera" (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria). Given the combination of diabetes, thromboembolism, and the pathognomonic necrolytic migratory rash, glucagonoma is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves surgical resection of the tumor and somatostatin analogs to control symptoms

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In hemodialysis-associated amyloidosis, which specific biochemical type of amyloid is deposited?
questions.explanation: Amyloidosis involves the extracellular deposition of misfolded fibrillar proteins in various tissues. In patients undergoing long-term hemodialysis, a specific type of amyloidosis develops due to the accumulation of Beta-2 microglobulin, labeled as Aẞ2m (Option C). Beta-2 microglobulin is a component of the MHC Class I molecule and is normally filtered by the kidney. In renal failure, it accumulates, as standard dialysis membranes do not efficiently remove it. These fibrils typically deposit in osteoarticular structures, leading to carpal tunnel syndrome and joint destruction. AL amyloid (Option A) is derived from immunoglobulin light chains in plasma cell disorders. AA amyloid (Option B) is derived from serum amyloid A protein during chronic inflammation. ATTR (Option D) involves transthyretin and is seen in senile systemic or familial amyloidosis. Therefore, Aẞ2m is the definitive biochemical marker for dialysis-related amyloid deposits

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient was provisionally diagnosed with intestinal obstruction. An emergency laparotomy was done, and the following specimen was removed. Identify the following specimen.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trichobezoar

The given specimen is that of a trichobezoar. This is a type of bezoar that forms in the stomach due to the accumulation of hair.

Trichophagia is the compulsive eating of hair associated with trichotillomania. Trichotillomania is a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder that is associated with hair pulling. In trichophagia, people also ingest the hair that they pull.

Complications of trichotillomania include

* Trichobezoars

* Malnutrition

* Intestinal obstruction

The modalities currently used in the management of trichotillomania are cognitive behavioral therapy and habit reversal training.

Other options:

* A phytobezoar forms when undigested plant material, such as fibers from fruits and vegetables, clump together in the stomach and create a mass that can lead to gastrointestinal symptoms.

* Lactatobezoar is a rare type of bezoar that forms in newborns' stomachs due to the accumulation of undigested milk or formula.

* Gangrene of the stomach can occur as a complication of conditions like gastric volvulus (twisting of the stomach), which leads to compromised blood flow to the stomach tissues.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the term used for a graft transplanted between genetically identical twins?
questions.explanation: In transplantation immunology, grafts are classified based on the genetic relationship between the donor and the recipient. An Isograft (or syngeneic graft) is a transplant between two individuals who are genetically identical, such as monozygotic (identical) twins. Because the MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) antigens are identical, there is no risk of immunological rejection. An Autograft (Option B) is a transplant of tissue from one part of a person's body to another (e.g., a skin graft). An Allograft (Option A) is a transplant between two genetically different members of the same species, such as a kidney from a non-twin sibling or a cadaver. A Xenograft (Option D) is a transplant between members of different species, such as a pig valve used in a human. Isografts represent the ideal transplant scenario because they achieve permanent survival without the need for lifelong immunosuppression

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A newborn presented to the NICU with respiratory distress and meconium discharge from the umbilicus. The condition occurs due to the patency of the which structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitellointestinal duct

The presence of meconium discharge at the umbilicus is suggestive of vitelline fistula, which occurs due to patent vitelline duct, which connects the primitive gut to the yolk sac.

The primitive gut is connected to the definitive yolk sac through a narrow stalk-like communication known as the vitellointestinal duct. It is also known as vitelline duct or yolk stalk or omphalomesenteric duct.

Due to the folding of the embryo in the cephalocaudal and lateral directions, the embryo gets enclosed all around by ectoderm, except in the region through which the vitellointestinal duct passes. In this region, there is a circular aperture, which is now called the umbilical opening. The vitellointestinal duct completely obliterates by the 7th week of development.

Vitelline duct abnormalities:

* Meckel's diverticulum: In about 2% of the individuals, a portion of the vitelline duct persists an outpouching of the ileum called, Meckel diverticulum. The diverticulum is usually asymptomatic unless it contains heterotopic pancreatic or gastric mucosa, which may lead to bleeding, ulceration, or perforation.

* Vitelline cyst: In some individuals, both the ends of the vitelline duct transform into fibrous cords. However, the middle portion of the duct forms a large cyst called, enterocystoma, or vitelline cyst. As the fibrous cords run across the peritoneal cavity, it may lead to intestinal obstruction, strangulation, or volvulus.

* Vitelline fistula: When the vitelline duct remains patent over its entire length, it forms a direct communication between the primitive gut and the umbilicus, a condition called an umbilical fistula or vitelline fistula. The newborn characteristically presents with meconium discharge from the umbilicus.
questions.learning: Vitellointestinal duct — The presence of meconium discharge at the umbilicus is suggestive of vitelline fistula, which occurs due to patent vitelline duct, which connects the primitive gut to the yolk sac.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient after a road traffic accident presents to the emergency room with difficulty in swallowing and slurred speech. Investigations reveal fractures in the occipitotemporal region. Which of the following areas should be tested in order to find the nerve which is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the involvement of 9th and 10th cranial nerves due to occipitotemporal fracture and they are examined by testing the uvula which is marked as 2 in the given image.

The jugular foramen is located between the lower border of the petrous part of the temporal bone and the condylar part of the occipital bone. As the investigations reveal fractures in the occipitotemporal region, along with the history of difficulty in swallowing and slurred speech, are suggestive of injury to the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve passing through the jugular foramen.

Unilateral lesions of IX and X cranial nerves are commonly caused by skull-base fractures, strokes, or tumors.

Glossopharyngeal and Vagus nerve examination include:

• Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula(marked as 2 in the given image) at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
• The pharyngeal (“gag”) reflex is evaluated by stimulating the posterior pharyngeal wall on each side with a sterile, blunt object (e.g., tongue blade)

Patients with a proximal unilateral lesion of the vagus nerve complain of dysphagia. There will be a weakness of the soft palate muscles on the affected side. Attempts to voluntarily elevate the soft palate, like by asking the patient to say “aah” will reveal a weakness in elevation of the palate on the affected side. Along with this, there will be deviation of the uvula to the normal side, due to the unopposed action of palatal muscles on that side.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not a tributary of the thoracic duct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right jugular trunk

The thoracic duct is the main lymphatic channel of the body and drains lymph from both lower limbs, abdomen, left thorax, left upper limb, and the left side of the head and neck before emptying into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Its major tributaries include:

• Right and left lumbar trunks (via cisterna chyli)
• Intestinal trunk
• Left jugular trunk
• Left subclavian trunk
• Left bronchomediastinal trunk

The right jugular trunk does not drain into the thoracic duct. Instead, it usually drains into the right lymphatic duct or directly into the right venous angle.

Why Not the Other Options?

• Left lumbar trunk → Contributes to formation of the cisterna chyli.
• Right lumbar trunk → Contributes to formation of the cisterna chyli.
• Left jugular trunk → Drains into the thoracic duct near its termination.
• Right jugular trunk → Drains into the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old G2P1L1 presents with abdominal pain, bleeding per vaginum in labour and loss of fetal movements. She occasionally smokes but does not consume alcohol or recreational drugs. On examination, her pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 150/90 mm Hg and has a tense abdomen on palpation. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Abruptio placenta

The given clinical picture with abdominal pain, bleeding per vaginum, and loss of fetal movements in a hypertensive pregnant woman points to the diagnosis of placental abruption.

Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta is placental abruption.

Hypertension and smoking are important etiological factors in abruption. Hypertension leads to vasospasm of the placental blood vessels, which causes uteroplacental insufficiency.

The hemorrhage into decidua basalis causes separation and compression of the placenta. This leads to a compromise of circulation to fetus leading to fetal distress. The bleeding may escape through the cervix to cause external hemorrhage.

The common etiological factors for abruptio placentae include:

* Hypertension

* Preterm prematurely ruptured membranes

* Advanced maternal age

* Cigarette smoking

* Cocaine abuse

* Trauma

* Uterine fibroids

* Isolated single umbilical artery

* Short umbilical cord

* Prior abruption

* Subclinical hypothyroidism

* Placenta previa presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Hypertension is not a predisposing factor. High-risk factors include multiparty, previous cesarean, or myomectomy scar in the uterus.

* In preterm labor, fetal movements are not compromised.

* Hydramnios does not present with bleeding PV.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
An elderly woman presented with symptoms of confusion, thirst, and abdominal pain. On examination, she had pallor and thoracic spine tenderness. X-ray spine showed osteolytic lesions. Her lab investigations showed the following findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

• Hb - 6.9g/dL
• WBC 4000/cm3 with normal differential count
• Serum calcium 13mg/dL
• Creatinine 2.3mg/dL
• Total protein 9g/dL
• Albumin 2.4g/dL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Multiple myeloma

The given clinical scenario describes an elderly woman with confusion, thirst and abdominal pain along with elevated serum calcium levels (hypercalcemia), elevated creatinine suggestive of renal failure, anemia and osteolytic bone lesions (CRAB features); and hypoalbuminemia with elevated total proteins. The most likely diagnosis is multiple myeloma (MM).

MM is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia.

Signs and symptoms include bone pain (most common), pathological fractures, recurrent bacterial infections, normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated ESR, and normal ALP.

Electrophoresis shows monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin (M spike)

Urine analysis shows free kappa & lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

Peripheral smear shows rouleaux formation.

The diagnosis of MM is made by using the Revised International Myeloma Working Group criteria.

Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥10% (or) Biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma and any one or more of the following myeloma-defining events is required to meet the criteria:

Evidence of end-organ damage attributable to the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder, specifically: (CRAB features)

• Hypercalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL
• Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL
• Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL
• Bone lesions: One or more osteolytic lesions on skeletal radiography, computed tomography (CT), or positron emission tomography (PET-CT).

Any one or more of the following biomarkers of malignancy:

• Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60%
• Serum involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater
• >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is at least 5 mm or greater in size.

Treatment includes a combination of lenalidomide/thalidomide (immunomodulatory agents), bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor), and dexamethasone.

International Staging System (ISS) is used for assessing prognosis in multiple myeloma patients. Serum β2-microglobulin is the most important prognostic marker.

Other options:

Option A: The bony metastasis in breast carcinoma is usually osteolytic. However, CRAB features, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated total protein suggest multiple myeloma.

Option C: Primary hyperparathyroidism is characterized by hypercalcemia and low phosphorus but is not associated with anemia and hypoalbuminemia.

Option D: Milk-alkali syndrome occurs after ingestion of large amounts of calcium and vitamin D supplementation. It results in hypercalcemia, alkalosis, nephrocalcinosis, and nephrolithiasis.

questions.explanation: The image illustrates a Balloon Tamponade, a critical intervention for managing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) caused by uterine atony. Devices such as the Bakri balloon are inserted into the uterine cavity and inflated with fluid to provide mechanical compression against bleeding vessels in the uterine wall. An umbrella pack (Option B) is a surgical technique where a plastic bag filled with gauze is placed transabdominally to control pelvic bleeding after procedures like a hysterectomy. A parachute pack (Option C) is a variation of the umbrella pack that uses weighted pressure to control diffuse pelvic hemorrhage. Cervical ablation (Option D) is a treatment for precancerous lesions and has no role in the management of acute hemorrhage. Balloon tamponade is preferred as a first-line non-surgical option to stabilize patients and prevent the need for an emergency hysterectomy
